item.title: The Grief That Has No Funeral: Finding Peace After Pregnancy Loss
item.description:
It’s hard to know what to say after a pregnancy loss. And because we don’t know, we often stay quiet or say the wrong thing in hopes of offering some comfort. This grief gets folded up and tucked away because the world around us doesn’t quite understand where to place it.

We don’t have a gathering, and no announcement is sent out. People aren’t dropping by to offer meals and help around the house. Life keeps moving. There is no casserole brought to the door, no sympathy card in the mail, and no formally recognized time to step away from your daily life and mourn what was lost.

In the middle of this heartache, you’re left holding something hard to name. It could be an early pregnancy miscarriage, a stillbirth, or the loss of a baby shortly after delivery. The love you had for this baby is real, and so is the grief that accompanies the loss.

Women and families find themselves mourning in silence and pressed against a culture that tends to move on quickly. What seems like overreacting or being too sensitive is simply being a parent who lost a child, and that loss deserves a name.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

The grief of pregnancy loss is real, even without a name

One of the most heart-wrenching things about this kind of loss is the absence of language for it. There is no universally recognized title for parents who have lost a baby to a miscarriage or stillbirth, as there is with a spouse who loses a partner or a child who loses a parent. This absence of language creates a gap where grief can start to feel like something you’re not supposed to have.

Perinatal loss carries a deep grief that’s not determined by how far along a pregnancy was. There’s no question that emotional bonding begins the moment pregnancy is confirmed and sometimes long before. The excitement of planning for a child’s arrival is real.

But when it ends, grief will arrive with full weight as it does with any significant loss. It could be numbness, waves of unexpected crying, or a persistent emptiness that lingers daily. Some days feel manageable, and others, like a due date on a calendar or a baby shower invitation in the mail, can return everything to the surface without any warning.

Some Christian counselors specialize in this type of bereavement for parents. These counselors understand the complexity of this grief and how it is layered. This allows them to help parents move through this grief at their own pace.

Can a mother forget the baby at her breast and have no compassion on the child she has borne? Though she may forget, I will not forget you! – Isaiah 49:15, NIV

The Isolation That Can Follow a Silent Loss

When grief doesn’t have a public ceremony, people can feel alone. Friends and family are left unsure what to say, so they remain silent. Sometimes, coworkers are not informed of the pregnancy, resulting in a lack of acknowledgment of what was lost. It seems social media is inundated with announcements of healthy pregnancies and new babies, leaving you wondering where you belong.

The isolation that follows this loss is a natural response to grief that was never given room to breathe. Most of the time, it compounds over time, especially when a loss occurs more than once – the guilt and sense of spiritual abandonment that surfaces in isolation deserves to be witnessed. Holding grief on their own has a way of hardening and becoming a weight that shapes how you see yourself in your faith without even realizing it.

In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans. – Romans 8:26, NIV

How Faith Speaks Into the Pain of Pregnancy Loss

Christian women and families face spiritual wrestling with pregnancy loss. They question why it happened, whether their prayers were answered correctly, or if this is some punishment. These are legitimate questions, and they’re not a sign of weak faith. These questions reveal your heart, which is honest and engaged with its faith.

Scripture does not tell us to shy away from lament. We can read the book of Psalms for raw, unfiltered cries to God that don’t resolve quickly. This is our permission to take it all to God.

Faith isn’t asking us to process our grief in a tidy way. It simply suggests that we come as we are. That is not a small thing. In a world that expects us to manage, push forward, and perform, being welcomed into the presence of God without having it together first is an act of profound grace.

Many women find that, with the support of a Christian counselor, God is present in the loss. They begin to realize that God is never distant from the places that we hurt the most. He grieves with us, and the child that was lost was known by Him before the news of pregnancy became a reality. This carries a meaning that no cultural script can replicate.

Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart. – Jeremiah 1:5, NIV

Taking the First Steps Toward Healing

There is no easy or straight road to healing after a pregnancy loss. Unlike any other grief, there is no timeline and no comparison to someone else’s experience. The important aspect is that healing is possible, and you don’t have to find it alone.

Allowing yourself to grieve fully may look like creating a small memorial or writing a letter. Having a support group or others who understand the specific loss is one step toward healing.

It’s OK to permit yourself to feel something other than grief, such as joy or laughter, without interpreting that as a betrayal of the child you lost. Grief does not require permanence. It will shift, and as it does, allowing yourself to move with it rather than against it is part of what healing looks like.

Christian counselors are trying to help you identify what grief has done to your emotional health and your faith. They can walk you through rebuilding hope and faith without forgetting the loss. This allows you to make room for the loss in a life that continues to move forward.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NIV

Finding Peace

Pregnancy loss rarely gets a ceremony, but it asks everything of the people who carry the weight of this grief. It requires endurance in the face of silence and faith in the face of unanswerable questions. It asks for resolve in the face of a world that does not fully understand what was lost.

You are not required to minimize it to make others more comfortable. There is no requirement to perform recovery before you are ready. There is a God who numbers the hair on your head, and He knows and loves the child that you carried. This is a love that does not require public acknowledgment to be legitimate, nor does it require a certain number of weeks to matter.

Your grief is valid, your loss is seen, and the road to healing was not meant for you to walk alone. There is support available if you take the first step to reach out. You can contact a member of our reception team to get connected with the counselor who has faith-based approaches that will help with pregnancy loss and grief.

He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away. – Revelation 21:4, NIV

References:

https://www.choosingtherapy.com/perinatal-loss/

item.title: Hidden ADHD Symptoms in Adults
item.description:
So many adults are living with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and have no idea that this could be part of their struggles. This isn’t happening because ADHD symptoms are rare. It is because the symptoms do not look the way people expect. The hyperactive child bouncing off of classroom walls is the typical image that most people see when they think about ADHD.

However, in adults, the ADHD symptoms show up quietly and are often mislabeled as laziness, poor character, or anxiety. For adults who have spent years wondering why life seems harder than it should be, recognizing what ADHD actually looks like becomes life-changing.

Why ADHD Symptoms in Adults Look Different

The hyperactivity that defines ADHD in children shifts inward as people grow older. Adults tend to experience constant internal restlessness or a mental hum that never quite settles. Sitting through a meeting and trying to follow a conversation to its end or finishing a task before starting another doesn’t come from being disinterested. This happens because the brain has been wired to find stimulation in a different way.

The ADHD symptoms in adults are unnoticeable because adults have spent years developing systems, habits, and strategies to work around how much effort it actually requires to complete tasks.

The workarounds often show up as success. This increases the difficulty in identifying the symptoms. When a person has quietly restructured their life around ADHD, they may seem to be highly organized and high-achieving.

But the scaffold sometimes crashes, and the energy it took to look successful is exposed. A life event that brings changes to the home or work can bring significant damage. This is a time for seeking answers because the old system has given out.

The Symptoms That Nobody Mentions

Most know that difficulty focusing is part of ADHD. The surprise comes from newly diagnosed adults who have learned the range of symptoms that never made it onto the checklist they imagined. One of the most significant aspects is the person’s ability to maintain emotional regulation. It is the least discussed symptom of adult ADHD.

There is an intense emotional pain triggered by perceived criticism or failure called rejection-sensitive dysphoria. This can be so overwhelming that it will shape every relationship and career decision a person makes.

This dysphoria can do more damage than other focus-related symptoms. It does not take much – a facial expression, a canceled plan, a conversation that felt off. The emotional response can be swift and intense – and for most adults who experience it, the safest thing they have learned to do is act like it didn’t happen. Hiding becomes its own kind of exhaustion.

Another common ADHD symptom among adults is time blindness. This symptom shows up as an experience of time existing only in categories: now and not now. Deadlines, commitments, and appointments are abstract until they are suddenly urgent.

The flipside of this is hyperfocus. This happens when an adult locks in with extraordinary intensity on something engaging for hours. This leads to skipping meals and going without sleep. None of these symptoms is what most people see as common ADHD distracted behavior.

Hyperfocus gets mistaken for a superpower sometimes. And honestly, it can be. But it has a dark side. That same intensity can latch onto the wrong thing at the wrong time – and once it does, good luck redirecting it. The garage gets completely reorganized on a Saturday while an urgent work deadline sits untouched. The deadline doesn’t move. The brain does what it wants anyway.

ADHD Symptoms, Shame, and the Spiritual Weight They Carry

Christians with undiagnosed ADHD carry a different kind of burden. They feel as though the inability to follow through on commitments and their chronic disorganization get filtered through a moral lens instead of a neurological one.

Many of these individuals may end up internalizing the message that they are undisciplined or spiritually weak. This is a real issue that carries a real weight for some individuals. The internal critic that comes with it can be relentless. For believers, it often speaks in the language of faith.

Not every faith community knows how to hold this. The language of discipline and self-control runs deep in Christian spaces. But for someone who has spent years wondering why those things feel so far out of reach, the Sunday morning message can quietly become one more area where they feel like they’re falling short.

God’s word speaks to the mind that feels scattered and overwhelmed. In Philippians 4, the anxiousness and restless thoughts should be brought to God in prayer and trust that His peace will guard their mind. This brings hope for those who have felt like their brain has been working against them (Philippians 4:6-7). Just because it’s a neurological difference does not mean it will disqualify the adult with ADHD from receiving this peace. It just looks different.

How ADHD Symptoms in Adults Affect Relationships and Daily Life

Undiagnosed ADHD does have a relational impact that can be significant and painful. Partners of those who have ADHD symptoms feel unheard and deprioritized. At the same time, the person with ADHD feels as though they are carrying genuine love alongside a brain that loses track of details or forgets conversations.

There are times when a friendship may fade because maintaining contact requires a sustained low-stimulation effort. This can prove to be hard for an adult with ADHD.

None of it means they don’t care. The forgotten plans, the faded friendships, the conversations that slipped – that’s not indifference. That’s a brain with a full tank that somehow keeps running dry. Explaining that gap to the people who got hurt by it may be the hardest part of all.

In the workplace, these adults often feel like they are on a pendulum that swings back and forth between the alignment of the environment and the ADHD brain function. Other areas that can prove to be strenuous include financial management, long-term planning, and household organization.

In Scripture, Paul wrote about the experience of knowing what is right and the act of actually doing it. This is something that resonates deeply with many adults who grapple with this gap between intention and follow-through that ADHD has produced (Romans 7:15-20).

The gap between intention and follow-through is not a moral failing. Paul felt it. Adults with ADHD live with it. Unlike some gaps, this one can actually narrow. But it requires the right understanding and the right support behind it.

How does Christian counseling help?

Recognition alone does not resolve the years that have been spent struggling with ADHD symptoms. Professional support can be helpful with recognizing ADHD symptoms, as well as working through the relational strain and exhaustion that accompany the late diagnosis. Christian counselors are equipped to work with adults who are navigating ADHD in a way that addresses the practical challenges and the questions of identity, worth, and faith.

Good therapy for ADHD isn’t just about getting organized. It’s about dismantling a story someone has been telling themselves for decades. It is about removing the ideas that they’re lazy, that they’re not trying hard enough, and that they should just pray more. A faith-based counselor can hold the neurological and the spiritual in the same space. That combination is rarer than it should be, and it makes a real difference.

If you feel as though your life is on a pendulum between peace and anxious thoughts, your next step would be to reach out. Many Christian counselors can provide help from an informed and compassionate perspective on what ADHD symptoms look like in adults. They can also give tips on how to overcome them.

Contact our front office and speak to the reception team for more information. This will help you get started on the right pathway to understanding your brain and yourself much better.

References:

https://psychcentral.com/adhd/adhd-in-adults
https://www.webmd.com/add-adhd/adhd-adults

item.title: Considering Therapy? Discover Topics Covered in Therapy for Women
item.description:
Women are more likely to seek help for their mental health, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. This is good news. But you don’t have to wait until you feel like you can no longer bear a situation. Counseling centers use therapy for women for a multitude of topics.

Common Topics Covered in Therapy for Women

Women assume roles inside and outside the home. They serve as caregivers to families, friends, and the church. Many mothers and grandmothers also volunteer for organizations, including those in which their children or grandchildren are involved.

They pour out so much of themselves into others that they may not notice that they themselves are depleted. Hormonal shifts, life events, and other problems can take a toll on their physical and mental health.

We talk with women about a variety of topics at our center. The following are the common topics covered in therapy for women.

Trauma-Specific

Whether from abuse, neglect, abandonment, violence, or natural disasters, we see women trying to move past trauma. Trauma brings about nightmares, anxiety, depression, negative thoughts, fears, and a host of other issues. Trauma-specific issues often affect physical health.

Your counselor will get to know you and discuss a treatment plan for your specific situation while addressing you as a whole person. Christian counseling is more than just the mind. We want to help you thrive in your physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual health.

Body Image Issues

Body image issues can stem from societal pressures, childhood experiences, or sudden changes in body composition. However, not every thought is true. You should always challenge negative thoughts, a skill you can learn in counseling. Sometimes perception plays a huge role in how women view themselves. Body image issues can lead to body dysmorphia, eating disorders, and low self-esteem.

Relationships

Relationships with a significant other, parents, children, and extended family can cause distress if there is contention. Toxic relationships and friendships that leave you drained and feeling worse after being around them will erode your confidence. Some of these relationships feel painful. Counseling can show you how to be assertive and place distance if needed by teaching you how to set (and enforce) boundaries.

Life Events

One of the most common topics we cover in therapy for women is the transition into roles during major life events. All major life changes come with some stress, even the good ones. Stress and doubt may prevail as a woman tries to adjust or adapt to her new normal. Graduations, marriages, deaths, births, moves, and career changes can leave a woman feeling out of control and on edge.

Anxiety and Depression

Anxiety and depression are common mental health disorders we treat at our center. Chronic stress, hormonal changes, life changes, chemical imbalances, and other factors contribute to mental health conditions.

Arming a woman with strategies and techniques to overcome anxiety and depression and move forward is our goal. We want every woman to leave a session feeling empowered, not only by herself, but with God’s help.

Contact Us to Learn More about Therapeutic Approaches in Christian Counseling

Our office would love to work with you. Our representatives can connect you with a Christian counselor specializing in therapy for women. Therapeutic approaches can include talk therapy, group therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and more. Contact us today for an assessment.

Photos:
“Hands of young black woman”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

Read more at Considering Therapy? Discover Topics Covered in Therapy for Women | Everett Christian Counseling.

item.title: How to Care for Yourself in This Economy
item.description:
When we hear the term “self-care,” many of us think of spa days, resorts, and beach houses. And for many of us in this economy, those options are out of the question. However, there are several effective free or low-cost alternatives to help you care for yourself when you feel overwhelmed and stressed.

Daily Habits to Care for Yourself

You want to be healthy, physically, mentally, and spiritually. But how do you care for yourself during a downturn in the economy and busy days trying to make ends meet? The answer: you build daily habits into your life that are either free or low-cost.

The following are several tips you can try to care for yourself in this economy.

Make Movement a Part of Your Day

Movement does not have to mean grueling workouts at the gym for hours six days a week. Movement can be a few days of walking for 10 to 30 minutes and strength training every other day, three days a week. It can mean stretching before bed or Saturday morning Pilates. It can look like playing catch with the kids or walking the dog. Make it a part of your daily routine like brushing your teeth.

Stay Hydrated

Most people do not drink enough water to stay hydrated. Dehydration can lead to headaches, fatigue, rapid heart rate, and a drop in blood pressure. In extreme cases, dehydration can cause confusion, dizziness, fainting, kidney stones, and seizures. Depending on your climate, you may need to drink more than 64 ounces of water daily to stay properly hydrated. Consult with your physician.

Choose Your Meals Wisely

Ultra-processed foods can worsen anxiety and depression symptoms and trigger physical responses, like chronic inflammation. Caring for yourself includes eating nutritious foods to care for the body God gave you. Create a menu of healthy meals before grocery shopping to ensure you have what you need on hand.

Enjoy Green Spaces

There is something about standing in God’s green spaces, listening to nature, and inhaling fresh air. Green spaces have been shown to calm the nervous system. By sitting or strolling in nature, you activate the parasympathetic nervous system, calming the fight-or-flight response. Try to get outdoors more, whether it is to enjoy your morning coffee, during your lunch break, or for an after-dinner stroll.

Make a “Six Most Important Things” To-Do List

Mary Kay Ash, the founder of Mary Kay Cosmetics, had it right. She encouraged her consultants and directors to create a list of the six most important things to do the next day. This list narrowed focus and made it easier to get more done because people didn’t feel pulled in different directions while also keeping the list short. Create your list the night before, and move any tasks you do not complete to the top of the next day’s list.

Calm Your Nervous System

Triggering the parasympathetic nervous system is easier than we give it credit for. Most of us notice when we trigger anxiety, but pursuing calming hobbies and interests can be the catalyst for relaxing our bodies and minds. Consider pursuits like reading, listening to music, fishing, crocheting, or praying.

Serve the Community and Be Social

Serving the community may seem counterintuitive to caring for yourself, but volunteering to meet another’s needs can leave you feeling purposeful. Socializing with others at events, like church, the library, or local gatherings, keeps you from feeling isolated and provides opportunities for connection.

Create a Morning or Evening Basket

Start and end your day on a relaxing note by creating a morning or evening basket or comfort kit. Consider adding items that make you feel good and offer a few minutes of luxury. For example, you could include a bottle of lotion or a tube of hand cream, a novel, a puzzle book, a ball of yarn and a crochet hook, a devotional, or several herbal teas.

Get Help for Negative Thoughts

Negative thoughts have a way of sneaking in when you’re tired, overwhelmed, and stressed. Beat them at their own game by having a reframed mantra. First, identify the negative thought. Next, ask yourself whether this is really true, and flip the script by rewording the negative thought into a positive mantra to repeat aloud to yourself.

Help is Only a Call or Click Away

If chronic stress, overwhelming responsibilities, and worry about the state of the world have you feeling anxious or down, reach out to our office today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor. Your Christian counselor will address you as a whole: physically, mentally, and spiritually. Call or complete the online form today to get started. It is time to care for yourself so you can serve the Lord to the best of your ability.

The post How to Care for Yourself in This Economy appeared first on California Christian Counseling.

item.title: Severe Anxiety: Dealing with Medical Anxiety
item.description:
If you are one of the millions of people who suffer from medical anxiety, you know how crippling it can be. Logically, you may understand that seeking medical attention is the right thing to do to protect your health, but trying to get yourself to actually make and keep an appointment seems threatening and nearly impossible.

The difficult conundrum with medical anxiety is that it operates on an unfortunate and continual loop. When you fear the one thing that can stop the anxiety, it can make you feel not only trapped, but hopeless.

Can you get over medical anxiety? Yes, you can. Just like other fears and anxiety-based behaviors, through therapy and prayer, you can overcome these limitations and live a normal and healthy life. Read on to learn more.

What causes medical anxiety?

While you might be predisposed to anxiety through your biological makeup, most people aren’t born with this fear. It is something that develops after experiencing a medical trauma.

Maybe your beloved mother died of cancer, and now you fear every small anomaly you discover on your body. Or maybe you got an unfavorable diagnosis, and your anxiety has convinced you that every subsequent doctor visit will result in the same terrifying news.

There are a number of ways and reasons someone might develop medical anxiety. Whatever the cause, the resulting consequence is often insufficient healthcare, missed medical appointments, and delayed checkups. This can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle.

What characteristics make up medical anxiety?

Medical anxiety varies in type and severity. Some suffer from illness anxiety disorder (IAD), which is commonly known as medical anxiety or health anxiety. The definition, as given by the National Institutes of Health, is a psychiatric condition characterized by intense, persistent, and excessive fear of having or developing a serious, undiagnosed disease.

Some people have milder cases of medical anxiety and may simply refer to their condition as “white coat syndrome,” meaning they fear things related to doctors or medical facilities.

What does having medical anxiety actually look like? Here are some characteristics you might experience.

You catastrophize

If you have medical anxiety, you will likely assume the worst-case scenario is imminent for all things health-related. That little headache you have can become convincingly similar to a brain tumor. That skin tag, which is a normal part of aging, can look suspiciously close to a cancerous growth through the lens of anxiety. When you live in a constant state of threat, your brain scans for any new or additional information that could be a sign of a bigger threat.

You feel overwhelmed

Another unfortunate element of medical anxiety is the feeling of being overwhelmed. It’s not unusual for people to postpone routine checkups or visits for minor ailments. For those with medical anxiety, those missed appointments happen often and aren’t due to scheduling mishaps.

With every missed appointment, medical conditions can compound. A minor issue can develop into something more serious. When that happens, not only does the need to seek medical attention grow, but the fear of receiving devastating news grows right with it. Even if you want to get back on track with your health goals, seeing the number of appointments you would have to face can make the whole process feel like too much.

Your mind starts to reel as you recall the date of your last dental appointment. You notice your eyeglasses aren’t quite as effective as they used to be, and you don’t even remember the date of your last blood test. You know you should make those appointments, but trying to force yourself to do the thing you fear can feel nearly impossible, and the sheer number of these necessary appointments can feel overwhelming.

You’re preoccupied

When you suffer from medical anxiety, you have a persistent preoccupation or intense focus on having or contracting a serious illness. You may not have any real symptoms that would indicate imminent danger, but your anxiety reacts as if there is an actual risk.

You may try to comfort yourself by doing independent research on symptoms or early warning signs of danger. This information rarely brings peace and might easily trigger an even greater degree of anxiety.

You seek reassurance

Another common pattern in someone with medical anxiety is the constant need for reassurance. You might find yourself asking a spouse, family member, or friend if they think something is wrong with you. You go into painstaking detail about your symptoms, hoping they’ll tell you that you’re okay.

That works for a while. You feel relief, and your fears subside. But that peace is short-lived. Before long, the doubt will resurface, and you will wonder if they’re telling you the truth or if they are even confident in their own answer.

Your behavior changes

Your medical anxiety might not just affect your mind and emotions, but dictate your behavior too. You might excessively check for signs of illness, scanning your body for any anomalies or symptoms. Conversely, you might avoid medical offices and information altogether.

Getting Over Medical Anxiety

There may not be a magic switch that you can flip to suddenly feel fearless, but with slow retraining of your mind and body, you can learn to respond differently to your medical anxiety.

Therapy

One of the most effective ways to overcome this crippling fear is through therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can help you identify the thought patterns that fuel your anxiety and challenge them with truth. Instead of immediately jumping to worst-case scenarios, you can learn to pause and question those thoughts. You can also learn how to replace them with more realistic and reassuring ones. Eventually, this will weaken anxiety’s power over you.

Exposure therapy is another effective approach to overcoming medical anxiety. While exposure to the thing you fear the most might feel terrifying, you don’t have to force yourself into overwhelming and scary situations all at once. You can learn to take small, manageable steps instead.

Maybe you start by simply looking up a nearby doctor or scheduling an appointment. Even if you later cancel that appointment, you’ve made progress by exposing yourself to the idea of going to the doctor. Maybe you sit in the waiting room of a doctor’s office before you even make an appointment. Exposing yourself to the environment in a non-threatening way and knowing that your name won’t be called can help you build up a tolerance for medical environments.

Each step you take to expose yourself to medical situations can help build confidence. It trains your brain to feel safe, even when the threat feels imminent.

Trusting God

Much of the fear behind medical anxiety stems from a lack of control. You don’t know what’s going on inside your body, and that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But the good news is that God knows.

God created you wonderfully, and He knows every detail about you. While He never promised a life free of difficulty, He does promise His presence even in the face of adversity. When your brain starts to spiral into the “what ifs,” you can center yourself on what is the absolute truth. That God is with you and your life is ultimately in His Hands. Your lack of control doesn’t have to be a deficit, but can be viewed as faith.

Help For Medical Anxiety

If you need help getting past your medical anxiety, schedule an appointment with a Christian therapist. These professionals at this practice can help you overcome this crippling fear that not only affects your mind but can also impact your overall physical health. They can point you back to the all-knowing, all-powerful God who loves you and wants you not to live in this fear any longer.

Resources:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11211185/

item.title: The Benefits of Sleep: A Spiritual Discipline Worth Pursuing
item.description:
Have you ever thought at length about sleep? For several hours every day, we sleep and unplug from the world around us. We might drift into dreams, nightmares, or a restless sleep, and all the while the world carries on without us. There are many benefits of sleep, and sleep shouldn’t be something you treat as an optional extra or an inconvenience. It’s one of the Lord’s many blessings that helps us maintain our well-being.

Our Culture and Sleep

One of the things that most fitness apps and devices have is sleep monitoring. There’s a growing awareness that sleep is a significant part of a person’s health. That is often at odds with other aspects of our culture. Often, exhaustion is quietly glorified as packed schedules are seen as a sign of productivity. Admitting that you need more sleep can sometimes be read as a sign of weakness or a sign that you can’t keep up with the rest of the world.

For Christians, there’s an additional layer to all of this. Misreading the call to work diligently as unto the Lord can result in feeling like taking time to rest is self-indulgent or a failure of good stewardship. Yes, laziness is a reality, and Scripture warns us about it. For instance:

A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest – and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man. – Proverbs 24:33-34, NIV

The threat of poverty hanging over you on account of a little slumber could be enough to jolt you into constant activity, hustling daily, and staying on the grind ceaselessly. The warnings in Proverbs need to be understood in their context, as well as in the broader context of Scripture. Rest is considered a gift and a necessary part of faithful existence. The warning from Proverbs is part but not the whole of the story.

The rest of the story includes the reality of sabbath rest being woven into creation itself (Genesis 2:1-3), and taking time away from our labors was a command given to God’s people (Exodus 16; 20:8-11) patterned after God’s own ways of doing things. Even the land that people worked was supposed to be given a year of rest (Exodus 23:10-11). The Psalmist declares that:

In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat – for he grants sleep to those he loves – Psalm 127:2, NIV

Rest is not the same as laziness. More often than not, Scripture looks upon rest and sleep as a quietly defiant trust in a God who doesn’t slumber and is trustworthy. You can rest while resting assured that the One who holds it all together is keeping you safe and restoring you all at the same time.

Ways We Can Sabotage Our Sleep

There are some bad habits and unhelpful ideas regarding sleep that can end up sabotaging it. It’s helpful to identify the misconceptions or myths about sleep that can keep you stuck or make it harder for you to get your rest. Getting your mindset right about sleep will better position you to take hold of its benefits.

One mistake we can make is to minimize the role sleep plays in our lives. The seven to nine hours that sleep takes up each day are not dead space or unproductive time. Far from being a passive thing, sleep is one of the most metabolically active periods of the day. While you sleep, your body is doing some important work, including your brain consolidating memories, clearing out cellular waste products, and repairing tissue.

Another myth is the idea that you can stay busy during the week, and you can simply catch up on your sleep over the weekend. When you have a chronic sleep debt, that’s not something you can remedy in just two days. Sleeping in over the weekend certainly helps, but there is a physiological and cognitive cost to disrupted sleep. That cost accumulates in ways that a few extra hours of sleep can’t remedy. You need consistent sleep for that to happen.

You might also sabotage your sleep by not giving yourself adequate time for it. Not only is it important to get downtime before you actually sleep, but you then need to have enough hours of sleep each night. Some people can function well on less sleep, but that’s not most of us.

Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep so that they don’t wake up feeling groggy and can function at their best. Poor sleep hygiene can often result in getting irritable more quickly and not thinking clearly.

Simply getting to sleep on time can be a huge challenge. Whether it’s procrastination, getting caught up watching your favorite series, attending to your children or your chores, doomscrolling, or simply being restless thinking about the next day, it can be difficult to get to bed on time. If you don’t allow yourself enough downtime before bed, falling asleep with enough time to give you a full night’s rest might not happen.

The Benefits of Sleep

What does sleep actually do for you? One of the major ways you can motivate yourself to make changes that will help your sleep is to understand what the benefits of great sleep are. The changes that you may need to make can seem inconvenient, but the benefits you reap from good sleep make it more than worth it.

Some of the main benefits of sleep include:

Emotional regulation When you don’t sleep well, you may find yourself struggling to regulate your emotions as effectively as you do when you’re well rested. When you’ve slept well, you’re better able to respond patiently to conflict, you can manage your frustrations a bit easier, and you can face difficulty more optimistically.

Sleep helps a person address concerns such as irritability, a persistent low mood, or emotional reactivity. When you’re sleeping well, you’re in a much better position to face these challenges. You may notice that you are more patient, quick to listen, and slow to anger.

Physical well-being When you’re sleep-deprived, you’re at an increased risk for depression, anxiety, weight gain, and several chronic health conditions. Getting good sleep isn’t a cure-all for ailments, but it supports hormonal balance, better immune function, cardiovascular health, and your body’s ability to manage inflammation.

Spiritual wellness There are so many things to be anxious about as we go about our lives. We worry about work, our children, the state of our world, our health, and so much else. Going to sleep can be seen and practiced as a discipline. Hustle culture says that going to sleep can seem like a waste of time, but it can be a counter-cultural form of trust when we choose rest over productivity.

Going to sleep when it feels like the world is falling apart can be a huge step of faith. Not only is resting a good idea to help us gain perspective on things, but it can rightly be seen as an embodied acknowledgment that the Lord is God and we are not. The world doesn’t depend on our constant activity or vigilance. Rather, the Lord is the one who sustains all things, and He does not sleep (Psalms 121:1-8; Hebrews 1:3).

Getting a full night’s rest consistently can help to promote your well-being, emotionally, physically, and spiritually. What seems like a pointless surrender to inactivity for a few hours out of every day is actually one of the Lord’s greatest gifts to us. His invitation for us to rest, not only spiritually by resting in His perfect work through Jesus, but also physically by ceasing our labors, can help restore much-needed balance and wellness.

Next Steps to Get Great Sleep

When you want to make changes that last, the way to do that isn’t necessarily by making huge and dramatic overhauls. Making small but impactful changes and then sticking to them can make all the difference. Some places where you can start include the following:

Set a wake time Being consistent in when you wake up can make a significant difference in regulating your body’s clock. Choose a time when you’ll wake up and then stick to that for a couple of weeks before you move on to adjust other things.

Have a wind-down ritual For example, a forty-five-minute wind-down ritual can help if you find it hard to settle your mind before bed. This time is to allow your brain the time it needs to transition from the day’s activities toward the quiet of sleep. Your ritual could include dimming lights, stretching, praying and reading Scripture, or listening to gentle music. It’s best to put down your screens at this time.

Make your bedroom a place for sleep Your bedroom isn’t a multipurpose room, so if possible, avoid working or watching emotionally intense content there. The point is to create the association between your bedroom and rest, so when you’re in the room, you start to transition toward sleep much more easily.

Limit caffeine An afternoon coffee can still be active in your system around bedtime, so it’s important to cut yourself off about five to six hours before bedtime. Limiting energy drinks can also help your sleep.

Getting good sleep benefits you in many ways. Sleep can rightly be seen as a spiritual discipline, a way to surrender ourselves to God in a tangible way that also promotes our well-being. Struggling to sleep can be a symptom of depression, anxiety, or grief. If you find yourself experiencing sleep difficulties despite having good sleep habits, speak with a doctor or a counselor.

If you’re struggling with getting good sleep, you can reach out to our office to connect with a Christian counselor in Alamo Ranch, Texas, who can help you process some potential causes of sleeplessness.

item.title: Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy: Re-opening Closed Hearts
item.description:
Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFCT) is a highly effective, evidence-based approach that has become the gold standard for couples therapy. Built on the science of attachment theory, it was developed in the 1980’s by world-renowned psychologist and couples therapist, Dr. Sue Johnson.

Johnson posited that relationship conflicts and arguments are rarely about superficial issues. Instead, they are typically driven by a deep, underlying, often subconscious fear of disconnection, abandonment, or unworthiness.

Loving connection provides the dependable web of intimacy that allows us to cope with life and live life well. – Dr. Sue Johnson

The main focus of EFCT is to help distressed couples break the negative interaction cycles fueling their distress. It does this by addressing the underlying emotional needs and attachment patterns in the relationship, providing insight into why these dynamics exist, and teaching new ways of relating to one another. This is done with the goal of fostering deep emotional healing and the formation of a secure, lasting connection.

How It Works

According to Johnson, the conflict is never about the actual matter a couple is fighting about. Couples experiencing relational distress are struggling with basic attachment issues and unhealed childhood wounds they may not even be aware of. These can include feeling helpless, worthless, unlovable, inadequate, or abandoned.

As these underlying emotions get triggered and stirred up, it causes them to enter defense mode and close their hearts to each other. The signals they send tend to be distorted and misinterpreted. They may resort to anger, for instance, to try and get a response, or shut down to cope with difficult feelings or their partner’s reactions.

Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy is specifically designed to reopen closed hearts. It addresses the emotional disconnect, decodes negative patterns of interaction, and helps partners shift. They move from defensive, guarded positions to vulnerability and reconnection. They learn to reframe their arguments from perceived personal attacks to understandable responses to a sensed lack of emotional safety.

The therapist helps partners uncover the vulnerable emotions that lie deep below the surface. Together, they identify their masked attachment needs and start to understand how their attachment-related fears of loss are affecting their relationship. This helps them begin openly sharing their vulnerabilities with their partner to seek closeness and empathy, and new patterns of interaction are developed.

As they learn to become more empathetic, responsive, and attuned to each other, this leads to greater trust, emotional intimacy, and bonding. These changes foster deeper connection and attachment security.

The Science Behind Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Our relationships are not just emotional experiences. They are deeply rooted physical processes that continuously alter our brain’s wiring.

The need for a safe emotional connection with a loved one we can depend on is biologically wired into our nervous system. It is vital to our survival during infancy and times of crisis, as well as to the maintenance of our physical and mental health.

Functional MRI studies have shown that the presence of a secure loved one has a soothing effect on the nervous system. It calms the threat response and alters its neural activity in a way that fosters emotional safety and connection. Feeling rejected, isolated, or as though you do not matter, on the other hand, has a traumatizing effect.

Relationship distress is a survival-based reaction to the loss of connection. By helping couples identify and express their core emotional vulnerabilities, Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy enables them to rewire maladaptive emotional responses and restructure emotional experiences. Then they can rebuild connection and create a sense of emotional safety and trust.

What to Expect in an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Session

During an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy session, the therapist observes the dynamics between you and your partner. They take an active role in helping you identify the hidden vulnerabilities beneath the surface of your behaviors that are contributing to the conflict in your relationship.

A therapist also recognizes the recurring, predictable pattern of your fights in sessions. They help you learn to view this destructive pattern – not your partner – as the enemy, and guide you through new ways of interacting that foster a safe, secure connection.

The Three Stages of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Emotions are the foundation of human relationships. They influence the way we communicate and respond to one another. When our emotions are acknowledged and validated, we feel heard and understood, and our satisfaction with the relationship is enhanced. On the other hand, when partners ignore or dismiss them, it can lead to conflict, disconnection, frustration, resentment, and destructive interactions.

EFCT consists of nine specific steps, divided into three stages, that help guide couples through a process. These steps help them become attuned to subconscious emotions and unmet needs, reprocess their distressed responses, and transform negative patterns of interaction into positive, secure attachment bonds.

Stage 1, De-Escalation (steps 1-4): In this first stage, the therapist lays the groundwork for change by tracking the way you and your partner interact. They help you become aware of your negative patterns of behavior, such as criticizing, attacking, being defensive, withdrawing, or shutting down.

They work to help you understand the deeper emotions and unmet needs that are triggering these behaviors, see how your insecurities and fears are impacting your relationship, and redefine the problem as being the negative cycle you are caught up in rather than blaming each other for it.

Stage 2, Restructuring Emotional Bonds (steps 5-7): This stage is devoted to creating a sense of security and restoring the emotional bond between you and your partner. The therapist guides you through new interactions that promote emotional engagement and move you beyond defensive reactions to more authentic communication.

In this, you learn to be vulnerable with each other, share deep underlying emotions and needs without fear of being judged, respond in supportive, empathetic ways, and engage in constructive dialogues with one another rather than destructive arguments.

Stage 3, Consolidation (steps 8-9): In this last stage, the therapist helps you and your partner integrate what you have learned into your day-to-day interactions and rehearse the skills you have developed to solidify these new patterns. You can practice comforting and connecting rather than disconnecting in the face of challenging emotions.

Specific Techniques Used in Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Trying to change your behaviors without dealing with the unspoken issues that lie beneath the surface of your responses is ineffective, which is why EFCT is not just about better communication. It is about helping you identify and address these underlying emotions and share them with your partner.

The following are examples of the types of techniques used to enhance emotional awareness, facilitate the expression of previously disowned needs and feelings, and encourage deeper connection, empathy, and understanding between partners to create a deeper emotional bond.

Emotionally Focused Conversations: An emotionally focused conversation is a structured dialogue that helps create an environment of empathy and compassion in which each partner is encouraged to discuss his or her thoughts and feelings without being interrupted.

Hold-Me-Tight Conversations: A hold-me-tight conversation is a guided dialogue that encourages partners to be vulnerable and share their deepest fears and needs, and talk through how they each hear the revelation. It aims to slow down the negative interactions and help the couple become more empathetic, emotionally responsive, and engaged with one another, transforming relational distress into emotional connection.

Reflection and Validation: Reflection and validation are techniques used to help couples recognize and articulate their needs and feelings by deepening their self-awareness and helping them recognize and process their hidden emotions.

Using empathic supposition, the therapist mirrors their words back to them in a clearer, more detailed way. They highlight core meanings or name emotions to help them see perspectives they may have missed, validate their experience, and reinforce its importance in the relationship.

Attachment-Focused Interventions: In attachment-focused interventions, the therapist helps partners recognize their attachment style and how it is influencing their interactions. They gain insight into their emotional responses and learn to navigate relational challenges in a healthier, more effective way.

Enactments: Enactments are role-playing exercises that help couples practice the new communication skills they have learned in a supportive, non-judgmental environment under the guidance of the therapist.

Are you interested in learning more?

If the information in this article resonates with you, and you would like to set up a risk-free appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors at our location, please give us a call.

References:
Marni Feurman. “How Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) Is Used.” Verywell Mind. Updated December 3, 2025. verywellmind.com/emotionally-focused-therapy-for-distressed-couples-2303813.

item.title: What Many People Misunderstand About Borderline Personality Disorder
item.description:
If you have ever had an exposed nerve ending in your tooth, you will know how painful and miserable an experience that can be. Although you could not see the issue, you would have been aware of it every time you chewed food on the side of your mouth where the nerve was exposed. Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is like having multiple exposed nerves that cause overwhelming emotional pain most of the time.

Simple events can feel devastating. You live with a constant feeling that your loved ones are going to leave you, and you often experience overwhelming mood shifts. Your nervous system is in deep distress, and there is no equivalent of a dental filling to protect your emotions from the pain.

When you live your life as an impulsive, reactive, deeply emotional person, your relationships cannot help but be affected. Not only are relationships more complicated with Borderline Personality Disorder, but you frequently experience the one thing you fear the most: people leaving you.

Some people simply do not have the capacity or the compassion to stick by you. Other times, you push people away because of how BPD affects your view of others. You either see people as shining examples of everything right with humanity or as the devil incarnate, incapable of being good.

Borderline personality disorder is a mental health condition defined by black-and-white thinking, this or that, with no in between. It is exhausting to live experiencing such extremes, and most people with BPD are internally exhausted from having to experience everything they do. However, it is possible to recover from BPD, to learn to have emotionally stable relationships and friendships, and to be emotionally regulated. It is a long journey that begins with understanding yourself.

The Diagnostic Criteria for Borderline Personality Disorder

People who suspect they have BPD generally display the following symptoms for years: a history of instability in relationships, regular, extreme angry outbursts, impulsive behavior with disruptive consequences, and frequent, intense mood shifts. Behavioral traits like these might be attached to several trauma-related experiences, like PTSD or CPTSD. A mental health expert can confirm an official diagnosis of BPD if five of the following nine symptoms are ongoing and disruptive to your life.

(Note that this is not a tool to self-diagnose, or to diagnose someone else, but it is simply the diagnostic criteria that psychiatrists use to determine Borderline Personality Disorder.)

Frantic Attempts to Avoid Abandonment

With BPD, it constantly feels like people are preparing to cut you loose from their lives. Things as simple as an unanswered text message or a perceived change in mood cause you to spiral and to do whatever you can to avoid the seemingly inevitable abandonment. This could mean even threatening suicidal behavior as a way of getting their attention and keeping them from leaving you.

Unstable and Intense Relationships

People with Borderline personality disorder can only see others through a black-and-white lens, with no neutral shades. This means they see others as entirely good or entirely bad, with no blending of traits.

As if this were not unhealthy enough, there might be a random moment when their view of someone suddenly flips. They go from having that person placed on a pedestal to villainizing their every action. This makes for turbulent relationships and connections with others, ironically ensuring that others abandon them, just as they anticipated.

Identity Disturbances

Just as they see others in terms of black-and-white judgments, their sense of self-worth is similarly extreme. They tend to either feel like the most important person in the room or the most worthless, with the tendency to flip from one to the other with little warning. Along with rapid shifts in their self-esteem, their preferences, interests, and values continually change too.

Chronic Impulsivity

People with BPD have frequent, disruptive, impulsive behavior, which causes a variety of issues. From excessive spending to making major life choices on a whim to engaging in harmful behavior with others, this impulsive behavior is as destructive as it is unpredictable. The issue with chronic impulsivity like this is that there are often long-term consequences, and some of them are difficult to walk back.

Extreme Mood Swings and Instability

A person with BPD can go from a state of euphoria to anger and to anxiety over the space of a week. They experience each mood intensely for up to two days before moving on to the next mood. Of course, none of it is intentional, and they often know that none of the emotions are rational while feeling them. However, trying to regulate such intense emotions is like trying to calm a tsunami wave.

Chronic Feelings of Emptiness

After several dramatic mood swings, a person with Borderline personality disorder usually comes back to a baseline of feeling lonely, bored, and empty. Loneliness and emptiness are sometimes so intense that they become suicidal or resort to self-harm to feel something different. Some people with BPD describe their most stable, constant moods as being lonely or numb.

Extreme Anger That Is Hard to Control

Anger is often a logical response to injustice or unfairness. However, for the person with BPD, anger is most often disconnected from current events or is a disproportionate response. It frequently leads to physical aggression and threats, often with dire consequences.

Feeling Disconnected From Reality

When not feeling irrationally angry, empty, or on an emotional roller coaster, people with BPD tend to dissociate from reality. They might feel an out-of-body experience, or as if nothing around them is real. This mood does not persist for long, but it is unnerving each time it happens.

Repeated Crisis Behaviors Under Stress

More than most people, those with Borderline personality disorder engage in self-harm and suicidality when under stress. This behavior ranges from threats to suicide attempts, and overdoses on medication. It is often because they feel overwhelmed by the feeling of loneliness that they resort to these actions.

Recovery and Hope for a Future

All is not lost for those with Borderline Personality Disorder. Many people who spent decades struggling with the disorder eventually improved to the point of no longer meeting diagnostic criteria. It is not an easy or fast road, but with a combination of the right medication, therapy, and determination, it is possible that you can make as full a recovery as you could hope for.

It is helpful to know some terminology that is part of the recovery journey with BPD, however. If you have incorporated counseling or therapy as a regular part of your mental wellness, you might experience symptomatic remission. This is when you have become stable and no longer meet the diagnostic criteria for Borderline Personality Disorder.

This is an achievement to celebrate, because it means that you have conquered much already. At this stage, it is advisable that you still receive counseling and support for your mental health, as some people experience relapses even when they thought they had recovered.

Recovery comes several years after symptomatic remission. When you have been asymptomatic for years, when you have managed to participate in several balanced, long-term relationships, and have had no disruptions from unruly emotions, you can finally say that you have recovered. The point is that recovery is possible and that it is worth the effort, focus, and perseverance it takes to achieve.

It can often feel like you are too damaged to heal, or that too much has happened ever to be able to experience stability and calm. Both feelings are valid, but the truth is far more optimistic. You can have a life without exhausting emotional swings; you can have relationships without excessive drama, and you can find love without fear of losing it. You just need to ask yourself if you are willing to risk the journey to find it.

Borderline Personality Disorder is not easy to deal with alone. We host an online catalog of counselors where we hope you will find someone to walk with you. Alternatively, our reception team can help you find a counselor according to your specifications and preferences.

item.title: Perfectionism and Anxiety: Is Pride Just Insecurity in Disguise?
item.description:
Some of the most prideful people are often the most insecure. There’s a common misconception that prideful people are bold, arrogant, and think quite highly of themselves. Of course, this is true in many cases, but it may not be typical.

More often, pride comes out of insecurity. Pride manifests in the places where people are the most unsure of themselves or are the most afraid of being exposed. Pride really shines in those fragile parts of their lives where they’re the most desperate for approval.

Pride and insecurity might look like opposites on the surface, but if you dig deep enough, you’ll find that they often share the same root. Someone who is insecure will often try to prove that they are worthy. Outwardly, this looks like confidence, but it’s actually more of a defense mechanism.

Insecure Pride as a Defense

Pride can be difficult to spot sometimes because it wears a lot of different masks. One of those masks is defensiveness. In the real world, this might look like someone’s need to win every argument or to be looked upon as the smart one in the friend group. It could also manifest as a refusal to apologize or to admit weakness. Sometimes it even shows itself as perfectionism and anxiety.

Someone who appears prideful might actually feel inadequate, and they might become highly critical of others. If they can’t measure up to the accomplishments of someone else, they might criticize and try to bring that person down to their level.

Prideful people also have a difficult time apologizing or admitting their own mistakes. They might cover up their failings or try to project them onto someone else. This can manifest as phrases such as “You made me do it” or “If you hadn’t done that, I wouldn’t have done this.” Prideful people rarely take responsibility for their own failures because they don’t want to add another mistake to what they believe is an already lengthy list of their flaws.

As destructive as they are, prideful behaviors are sometimes praised and admired because they can look quite attractive. They might look like confidence to the world, a trait often praised in our society. This praise reinforces the behavior because it also feeds the person’s ego. This creates a cycle of behavior. But when you look a little deeper, under the fake confidence, you will likely see that these behaviors are protecting fragile self-esteem.

The Cycle of Pride

When someone fears being rejected, they might present themselves as superior in an attempt to convince themselves and their audience of their worth. Because they don’t believe they can meet someone else’s standard, they puff themselves up, trying to appear better than others.

Pride and insecurity are both part of a larger cycle. Insecurity creates a fear of exposure. Protective pride in the form of arrogance or perfectionism creates a temporary ego boost, which pressures you to maintain this false mask. And the knowledge that you’re falsely elevating yourself or are inauthentically being propped up by others creates even deeper insecurity.

Pride in the Bible

The Bible has quite a lot to say about pride. Scripture consistently warns that pride can lead to a destructive path. Proverbs 16 tells us plainly that “Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18, NIV)

What does pride mean in this context? In this passage, pride does not refer to confidence or feeling good about yourself. Feeling confident in the creation God made you to be is not a detriment, but a goal. Biblically speaking, pride refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It is a posture of the heart that believes it’s better than anyone and doesn’t need correction.

The Hebrew word used here in Proverbs for pride is gaon. At its core, it means height or majesty. When used negatively, as it is in this context, it refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It’s the idea of rising above others in a falsely elevated way.

This can happen through arrogance, prideful elevation of oneself, self-exaltation, or a sense of superiority. Proverbs 16:18, in the original text, also uses a related idea, ruach gavoah, which means a high or lofty spirit. Together, these terms paint a picture of someone who has lifted themselves to appear more important than they actually are.

Having pride has become a badge of honor in modern culture. Biblically, elevation belongs to God, not us. By puffing up (gaon), we create an attitude that eventually causes the fall that Proverbs warns about.

Scripture also helps us understand that pride can hide insecurity. In Luke 18, Jesus tells a story about two men who went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, a man who would have been respected in his day for his religious devotion. The other was a tax collector, someone whom most of his contemporaries would have called corrupt.

The Pharisee prayed confidently: “‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people, robbers, evildoers, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.’” (Luke 18:11-12, NIV)

The tax collector took an opposite posture. Scripture says he stood at a distance and wouldn’t even look up to heaven. He didn’t have a long and eloquent prayer, but simply said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, NIV)

The result might surprise you. The tax collector, not the prideful Pharisee, went home justified before God (Luke 18:14) because the tax collector was honest. He wasn’t comparing himself to anyone or trying to prove his worth. He simply admitted his need while the Pharisee was busy defending his own worth.

Pride Is Exhausting

Maintaining an image, like the Pharisee in our example, takes a lot of effort. If your identity depends on appearing strong, capable, or morally superior, then you are constantly attempting to manage how others see you.

Every interaction or conversation, the ones most people don’t give much thought to, becomes heavily important when you are protecting your curated image. Constructive criticism is viewed as an attack, and every mistake is seen as an enemy. That responsibility can be downright exhausting.

God Is Our Peace

What brings peace and can quiet those insecurities and squelch that pride?

Humility is often misunderstood. Many people assume that humility is thinking poorly of yourself. But that’s not biblical humility at all. Humility is simply seeing yourself accurately. It is the ability to recognize your strengths without exaggerating, as well as your weaknesses without cover-up. This accurate self-assessment actually creates emotional freedom.

Humility recognizes grace. When you can admit your frailties, limitations, and mistakes, you leave room for God’s forgiveness and grace. Your IQ, test score, paycheck, or social media presence isn’t going to ever be good enough to get you to Heaven.

“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith – and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God –  not by works, so that no one can boast.” (Ephesians 2:8-9, NIV) That realization alone can be humbling and remove the need for pride.

Therapy Can Help

Many prideful behaviors stem from old insecurities. Maybe the mistakes you made as a child were harshly criticized or constantly compared to others. Pride then can become a shield or a way to compensate for that lingering sense of inadequacy.

Therapy can help you trace your prideful behaviors back to their roots. When you stop trying to maintain a perfect image, you open yourself up to growth. You can finally deal with the underlying issues. When you do this, something beautiful and authentic happens.

You will begin to feel safe enough to acknowledge your own limitations, fears, or weaknesses. You will find a place of humility. And with this self-actualization, the need for pride and the perfectionism and anxiety that often come with it will start to fade, leaving room for the awesome work God wants to do in you.

If you need help addressing issues of insecurity or pride, call our offices and make an appointment. Specially trained therapists can help you grow in your humility and embrace the grace of a God who does not require perfection.

Resources:
https://biblehub.com/lexicon/proverbs/16-18.htm
https://enduringword.com/Bible-commentary/luke-18/

“In the Kitchen”, Courtesy of Chang Duong, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; 

The post Perfectionism and Anxiety: Is Pride Just Insecurity in Disguise? appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Relationship Issues: When You Feel Replaced
item.description:
There comes a time in almost every relationship when one, or perhaps both, parties worry about being “replaced.” Of course, you’re irreplaceable, and you might even know down deep that your unique qualities make it impossible for someone to replace your role in another person’s life. But down deep, you might also wonder if your role in your sibling’s or friends’ lives is being taken over by someone else.

These feelings of jealousy and insecurity can lead to some really serious relationship issues.

There’s someone new in the picture

By nature, most people thrive in the familiar. That’s why many of us love being at home, surrounded by familiar and comfortable things, like our favorite sounds and smells. And of course, we love our familiar people too.

Family members and good friends are a beloved part of your life. You treasure their company and rely on their companionship to get through difficult days. Of course, they annoy you, as you do them, occasionally, but these people, your people, are a foundational part of your life.

Enter someone new.

What could upset this beautiful life, these familiar people and surroundings? A new person.

Why are they a threat?

Uncertainty and unfamiliarity are often a threat to our peace. When someone new enters a friend group, a neighborhood, or your life in any capacity, you don’t know how to contextualize them yet. Are they going to be your new best friend? Are they going to be a threat to your marriage? Are they going to be a temporary acquaintance that you won’t remember six months from now?

But as you get to know these new faces, sometimes they start wiggling their way into your life in a more concrete and consistent way than you expected. It’s great at first. They’re a wonderful addition to your group of friends, family, or work environment. But somewhere along the way between acquaintance and bestie, there is a dynamic shift.

Soon, your friends are accepting of this new person. Your parents start dismantling those solid social walls that they’ve had up for years. Your sister, who is known for being introverted, is suddenly comfortable with this new person. Your work friend is suddenly shifting all their attention to this new, novel friend.

And while you might like this new person, maybe even a lot, you start to wonder if they’re the new you. Are they going to fulfill your role in your relationships, shoving you right out the door?

Am I a bad person?

When you start resenting someone else who is getting close to your favorite people, it’s natural to have alarms go off in your head. But does that make you a bad person? No, it makes you human.

Anytime something important gets threatened, your natural fight-or-flight mode kicks in. In this context, your feelings of danger activate your instinctual desire to either fight for your place in your group of friends or your family, or to get as far away from that person as possible.

So, while this response might make you look like and most likely feel like a bad person, the truth is that this is not a reflection of your value. It’s a reflection of what you value.

Are they?

Is this person who is uprooting your life and threatening your social standing a bad person? Most likely, not. The likely scenario is that this person, the one who is muscling in on your life, is doing so because they, too, want to be accepted. They want to be a part of a healthy and exciting group of friends. Or they want to be accepted by the family.

While some people might have less than pure intent, most people are a nervous ball of insecurity with a need to be accepted. You know, just like you.

What do I do?

If you’re reading this, you likely feel threatened right now. Maybe your brother has a new fiancée, and you worry that she will “wow” the extended family. Maybe your best friend met a new person at work, and they’re spending a lot of time together. These new connections may feel less exciting to you than they do to everyone else. What should you do?

Whatever your situation, God is the solution

God’s love for you is not conditional. He will never prefer someone else over you or reject you when you want to spend time with Him. He loves you now and forever, and you don’t have to do one thing to earn that status.

And finding your identity in Him, really grounding yourself in the love of your Father, is a great way to overcome your feelings of rejection or the threats you might feel toward your human relationships.

The practical way to do this is to spend time with Him. Pour out all your insecurities and concerns to Him. Ask Him to bring the right people into your life, and to remove anyone who is truly harmful. Then trust Him for the solution.

Love them anyway

It can be difficult to love unlovely people. But it’s what you’re supposed to do. Of course, if someone is truly coming into your life with ill intent or is causing you any type of harm, you aren’t required to sacrifice your own safety and well-being to welcome them with open arms.

But if this new person does not have ill intent, then it’s best to put your own insecurities and concerns aside, leaving them in the Father’s Hands, and love this person. Try to see life from their perspective. Maybe they’re new in town, or maybe they just lost a loved one. Maybe they just enjoy meeting people and want to widen their social circle.

Maybe if you dropped your guard and didn’t feel the need to protect your position or territory, maybe you would find a good friend in this person too.

God wants us to love our enemies. That doesn’t mean you have to live in tandem with harmful people, but it means that you have to allow the love of the Lord to flow in and through you so steadily and abundantly that even those who are difficult to love see God through you.

Diversify

It’s possible that this new connection, as threatening as it might feel, is a good spotlight on your social life. Maybe this threat that you feel is not only showing you how much you love your people, but perhaps it is revealing something else.

If you’re so enamored and tied to someone that the thought of losing them throws you into an emotional rollercoaster, then maybe it’s time to diversify your friendships. Of course, this doesn’t apply to certain relationships like spouses, who should never put anyone else above you. But if you feel threatened by losing a friend group or someone special in your life, maybe you need to branch out into new social territory.

Volunteer at church, pick up a new hobby, or start frequenting that new coffee shop. When you meet new people, you will feel less threatened by losing those already in your life.

That’s not to say that you should give up on your current friendships. But it’s good to trust that the people who are truly meant to be there will remain, despite outside influences, and adding new people to your life can be both fun and rewarding.

Therapy for Relationship Issues

Are you struggling with the worry that you’re replaceable in the lives of your most important people? Therapy can help. Talking with a therapist can help you sort through the feelings of jealousy and envy.

It can open your eyes to past trauma, betrayal, and abandonment issues that might be contributing to your resentment. Therapy can also help you uncover insecurities and help you build confidence in yourself and as a child of God.

If you’re struggling with relationship issues or feel that you’re being replaced in the lives of your friends and family, call us today. A therapist will walk with you through these feelings and help you come through victorious, with a healthy view of your relationships and your place in this world, and find your identity in God. Contact our office today to learn more.
