item.title: Faith-Based Strategies for Men Who Struggle with Panic Attacks
item.description:
Men’s mental health is an evolving conversation, especially regarding the misunderstanding of men facing panic attacks. The episodes of a sudden rush of terror and racing heart create a collision between vulnerability and the expectations culture places on men. Anxiety symptoms in men do not manifest the same way as they do in women. This makes identifying and treating them more complex in men.

Most men of faith who experience panic attacks feel like it is a spiritual crisis as much as a mental health emergency. An internal conflict arises because of the contradiction between believing in God’s peace and experiencing overwhelming fear. This doesn’t indicate a lack of faith or weakness. It simply recognizes that mental health struggles require spiritual anchoring and practical intervention.

When faith-based approaches are combined with evidence-based mental health strategies, a pathway is created. This path honors both the spiritual and practical dimensions of recovery. Christian counselors know how to create faith-based treatment plans that cover both of these dimensions.

Do not fear, for I am with you; do not anxiously look about you, for I am your God. I will strengthen you, surely I will help you, surely I will uphold you with My righteous right hand. – Isaiah 41:10, NASB

Understanding How Panic Attacks Manifest in Men

Men don’t typically recognize the panic attack for what it is when they experience the anxiety symptoms. This is partly due to the message that men in this culture should be strong, independent, and emotionally controlled. The anxiety symptoms in men – chest pain, shortness of breath, or a rapid heartbeat – become the focus when they are experiencing a panic attack. Instead of acknowledging that it could be fear or worry, they are convinced they’re having a heart attack.

Men tend to externalize distress, often manifesting as anger, irritability, or aggressiveness. Some may report feeling as though they are out of control rather than stating they are anxious or scared. This pattern makes it hard for men and healthcare providers to identify panic disorders. Men are less likely to seek help for mental health issues or present them in a way that doesn’t fit typical diagnostic criteria.

Physical symptoms often dominate the male panic experience. Dizziness, muscle tension, sweating, a feeling of being choked, or difficulty breathing are the most common presentations in men experiencing panic attacks. Men who experience these symptoms often become hypervigilant about their physical health, leading to repeated medical visits. This creates a cycle that perpetuates the very symptoms they’re trying to avoid. Therefore, it is crucial to understand this pattern for men to break free from panic’s grip.

I sought the Lord, and He answered me, and delivered me from all my fears. – Psalm 34:4, NASB

Biblical Foundations for Mental Health Recovery

God’s word does not dismiss the human struggles or emotional pain that men experience. It directly addresses it through stories of people who experienced fear, anxiety, and challenging circumstances. In the book of Psalms, David writes about his fears, and Elijah experienced what is known today as depression and panic. Each of these accounts reminds us that panic has been a part of the experiences of the faithful throughout the ages.

Combining faith and mental health treatment doesn’t mean you choose one over the other. The approach of Christian counseling acknowledges that God works through various means, including therapy, medication, and clinical interventions. Faith provides the foundational understanding that healing is possible. Through this, prayer is not simply practicing mindfulness, but also a means of communing with the Heavenly Father, the eternal source of grace and strength.

Seeking help and guidance from others is a part of having and understanding biblical wisdom. Bearing one another’s burdens includes emotional and mental support. When men integrate their faith into panic recovery, they often find that faith-based practices don’t replace professional treatment. The peace we read about in the Scriptures isn’t the absence of difficult emotions, but rather the presence of God’s strength in the middle of the chaos.

Practical Faith-Based Coping Strategies

Daily quiet time and mindfulness offer men tools that can assist with managing panic symptoms. Faith-based quiet time isn’t the same as secular mindfulness, which focuses on emptying the mind. This quiet time involves filling the mind with the word of God through reading scriptures. At the onset of panic, men who practice breath prayers (deep breathing with short scripture verses) learn to regulate the nervous system and maintain spiritual focus.

From a faith perspective, Christians recognize their bodies as a temple of the Holy Spirit. Faith-based mindfulness helps with learning to notice the anxiety symptoms in men without judging their identity in Christ. Prayer and progressive muscle relaxation create a sense of groundedness that helps calm panic attacks.

Men may also find that community support within the church can provide a critical element in developing faith-based strategies. Men’s ministries and small groups can create space for men to be vulnerable and contradict cultural messages about male independence.

Sharing struggles about panic attacks in a safe Christian environment helps them know they are not alone. Strength is found in community, not isolation. The support system of the body of Christ is essential in providing strategies to overcome panic attacks.

Integrating Professional Christian Counseling

Christian integration in counseling sets our vision beyond merely coping with symptoms toward being conformed to the image of Christ. Every behavior, even distressing experiences such as panic attacks, serves a purpose and communicates something important about our inner world. In our work together, we will explore the depths of your anxiety to better understand what your panic is trying to express and invite Jesus into the storms that rage within your heart. The goal is for you to truly find rest in Jesus, even in the midst of suffering and uncertainty.

Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light. – Matthew 11:28-30, NASB

Christian Counseling can offer men an integrated approach that honors their faith and the need for professional mental health treatment. Licensed counselors understand that anxiety symptoms in men intersect with spiritual concerns and their masculine identity. They can help address the shame that men may feel about experiencing panic and provide evidence-based interventions. Acknowledging God through this dual approach often brings healing.

Some Christian communities hold a strong stigma around men seeking help for mental health issues. However, Christian counseling can help reframe this thought process as a stewardship of the mind and body that God has given. Seeing a doctor for a broken bone is no different than seeking Christian counseling for panic attacks. This can be seen as an act of wisdom rather than weakness, which will shift the perspective for men who struggle with the decision to pursue treatment.

Christian counseling can provide a therapeutic relationship and a safe space for men to explore the intersection of faith and mental health struggles. Some men have never been allowed to acknowledge that they can be faithful believers and struggle with panic attacks. Christian counselors help men understand this. This approach removes the false choice between faith and mental health treatment.

Listen to counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise the rest of your days. – Proverbs 19:20, NASB

Find Help Today

Faith-based strategies for men who struggle with panic attacks are part of the Christian counseling approach in recovery from panic attacks. This allows men to pursue mental health treatment without feeling as though they lack faith. Faith that meets professional care can lead to a deeper dependence on God and greater emotional maturity.

For more information on male mental health and overcoming panic attacks, reach out to your local Christian counseling office today.

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Dual Diagnosis
item.description:
What Does Dual Diagnosis Mean?

Technically, dual diagnosis (also known as co-occurring or concurrent disorders) means being diagnosed with two or more specific, co-existing conditions. This includes two mental health disorders, two physical illnesses, a mental health disorder and a physical illness, or a mix of mental, physical, and substance use disorders.

More commonly, however, the term dual diagnosis is used to specifically refer to someone struggling with both a mental health disorder and a substance use disorder at the same time.

What Is the Difference Between Dual Diagnosis and Co-Occurring Disorders?

Both terms typically mean the same thing and are often used interchangeably to describe two or more distinct disorders that exist concurrently. The key difference is in their scope.

Dual diagnosis generally has a more specific focus and has come to refer to the specific pairing of a mental health disorder and a substance use disorder.

Co-occurring disorders, on the other hand, is a more inclusive, umbrella-type term that covers a broader range of possible combinations that are not limited to the pairing of mental illness and substance use disorder. It can include more than two conditions, none necessarily substance abuse-related.

What Are Some Examples of Dual Diagnosis Versus Co-Occurring Disorders?

Examples of dual diagnosis include having both major depressive disorder plus alcohol or opioid addiction; post-traumatic stress disorder plus opioid or alcohol addiction; bipolar disorder plus addiction to amphetamines or cannabis; or generalized anxiety disorder plus addiction to prescription drugs.

Examples of co-occurring disorders include non-substance-related combinations such as major depressive disorder plus generalized anxiety disorder; schizophrenia plus obsessive-compulsive disorder; or bipolar disorder plus PTSD.

Is There a Link Between Mental Health Disorders and Substance Use Disorders?

Although substance use disorders may or may not directly cause mental health disorders, or the other way around, studies have shown that people with mental health disorders are more likely to have a concurrent substance use disorder than those who do not.

In people who do have both disorders, symptoms of one condition tend to make the other condition worse, and a key challenge is to determine whether one co-occurring disorder caused the other, or if they developed independently.

People with a mental health disorder, for instance, may self-medicate by using drugs or alcohol to help numb their symptoms and enable them to cope. This leads to a substance use disorder when the relief is only temporary. Then their symptoms become worse, and their body craves more and more of it to be able to function.

Substance use disorders, on the other hand, can trigger changes in brain structure, chemistry, and function, leading to the development of a mental health disorder or worsening the symptoms of an already existing one.

Left untreated, mental health issues can cause substance abuse to get worse, and an increase in substance use can cause mental health issues to worsen as well, creating a difficult cycle to break.

What Are the Most Common Co-Occurring Dual Diagnosis Disorders?

Some of the most commonly co-occurring disorders in a dual diagnosis include:

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by a persistent, unrelenting anxiety that tends to manifest as an irrational fear that takes over the person’s mind, often leading to a panic attack.

It is the condition most associated with self-medicating behavior and becoming reliant on prescription medications to help calm them down. Relief is only temporary, however, and does not treat the underlying condition. Eventually, more and more of it is needed to provide the same effect, and the person may use it in combination with alcohol or other drugs and develop a substance abuse disorder as well.

Bipolar disorder: Bipolar disorder is caused by a chemical imbalance in the brain and is characterized by severe mood swings between intense episodes of mania and high energy, and episodes of depression. People with bipolar disorder often turn to alcohol or other substances to help them cope with their intense feelings, which may provide temporary relief but worsen symptoms in the long run and cause the mood swings to intensify.

Major depressive disorder: Major depressive disorder and addiction are commonly linked. People suffering from it often turn to drugs or alcohol to help cope with their symptoms, but long-term, it causes the symptoms to get worse. Worsening symptoms lead them to need more and more of their substance to produce the same effect. In other cases, it is the substance use disorder that comes first and brings on the depression.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD): Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder is the result of experiencing or witnessing a terrifying event that the brain is unable to fully process, causing it to get stuck in danger mode. People suffering from it experience symptoms such as vivid flashbacks, nightmares, and feeling anxious and on edge even when there is no actual threat. Often, they turn to drugs or alcohol to help them cope with their racing mind and emotional distress, and numb their feelings of fear.

Schizophrenia: Schizophrenia is characterized by trouble distinguishing fantasy from reality. People suffering from it may be prone to disorganized thinking, delusions, and/or hallucinations. They often misuse drugs or alcohol to help them cope with their symptoms, which can worsen psychotic symptoms and interfere with treatment.

How Is Dual Diagnosis Treated?

The best, most effective treatment for dual diagnosis is a comprehensive, integrated approach that identifies and addresses both the mental health disorder and the substance use disorder simultaneously rather than separately. If only one condition is treated, the untreated one can interfere with progress, and the risk of a relapse after treatment ends is significantly increased.

Treatment needs to be individualized, as there is no one-size-fits-all approach. Depending on which substances and mental health disorders are involved, and how the symptoms of one are affecting the other, it may include inpatient care, behavioral therapy, medication, lifestyle changes, and/or peer support.

Inpatient care: Co-occurring disorders treatment centers provide comprehensive care that combines medical and mental health services, including medication management and therapy.

Therapy: The most commonly used therapies for treating co-occurring disorders include Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), which helps reshape negative thinking patterns by teaching you how to identify and reframe negative thought patterns; Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT), which focuses on emotional regulation, stress management, and reducing self-harm behaviors; and mindfulness-based techniques.

Medication: Drugs may be prescribed to help relieve the symptoms of one or both conditions, stabilize mood, and enable better engagement in therapy.

Peer Support: Peer support groups provide a safe space to connect with others who have experienced and understand what you are going through, get emotional and social support, and share experiences and tips for day-to-day challenges.

Are There Any Self-Help Tips That Can Help?

The following are some effective self-help tips that can help you sustain your recovery long-term.

Know your triggers and establish an action plan: Understand what your triggers are and have a plan for how to deal with them in a healthy way if you are unable to avoid them.

Stay connected with others: Having regular face-to-face contact with friends and loved ones, and being involved in a support group can help calm your nervous system.

Keep from making random changes to your treatment routine: Arbitrarily stopping treatment once you feel better is a common reason for relapse in people with co-occurring disorders. Always consult your doctor or mental health practitioner before changing your treatment routine.

Engage in healthy lifestyle practices: Engaging in healthy lifestyle practices such as regular exercise, relaxation and stress management techniques, healthy eating, and adequate sleep can help. These are natural ways to reduce stress or anxiety, improve your mood and outlook, and regulate your energy level.

Help with Dual Diagnosis

If you have questions about this article on dual diagnosis or need help navigating dual diagnosis, please call us today.

References:
“Dual Diagnosis.” Cleveland Clinic. Reviewed on August 5, 2025. my.clevelandclinic.org/ health/diseases/24426-dual-diagnosis.

item.title: When Faith Feels Like a Trap: Understanding Moral OCD and Christian Behavior
item.description:
For many of us, faith is meant to be a source of peace and direction. But what happens when that same faith becomes a source of relentless anxiety? What do we do when every thought feels like it needs to be confessed, and every decision requires certainty that never comes? How do we recognize the line between conviction and compulsion when it blurs beyond recognition?

This is a reality called moral OCD. It is a form of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder that affects our deepest values and turns them into a battlefield. As Christians, it can mean that our beliefs, meant to bring freedom, have changed with every prayer and every Scripture reading. With every attempt to do what’s right, we find ourselves battling an anxiety that we are just now understanding.

Moral OCD isn’t about being overly religious or having a sensitive conscience. It is when normal spiritual concern crosses into the territory where the mind becomes stuck in loops of fear and doubt. The first step toward finding healing for moral OCD is to recognize when a mental health disorder has hijacked our faith.

The Nature of Moral OCD

Moral OCD, sometimes called scrupulosity, is a subset of an Obsessive Compulsive Disorder that centers on fear about morality, ethics, and personal integrity. Instead of focusing on contamination or order, moral OCD targets our core values and beliefs.

This means it often manifests as overwhelming anxiety about sin, salvation, or offending God. We may experience intrusive thoughts that feel morally reprehensible and engage in a mental or behavioral compulsion to neutralize the anxiety that those thoughts create.

Intrusive thoughts are not reflections of character or desires. They are unwanted, distressing mental events the brain produces. This is where OCD latches onto them and demands certainty that we are still morally acceptable.

Those who suffer from moral OCD may replay conversations endlessly to ensure they didn’t lie, confess the same perceived sin repeatedly, or avoid situations where they may be tempted to think wrong thoughts. The compulsions will give temporary relief, but they also reinforce the cycle and teach the brain that these thoughts are genuinely dangerous and must be neutralized.

Moral OCD isn’t based on how devoted someone is to their faith, but it does exploit whatever a person values most. For Christians, that means moral OCD can transform genuine faith into a source of daily torment.

How Moral OCD Distorts Christian Behavior

Normal Christian practices become distorted when moral OCD takes hold. Prayer becomes a compulsion rather than a communion, and people repeat phrases until they feel right or confess the same fears over and over. Reading Scripture turns into a search for reassurance rather than an encounter with God’s character. Worship is driven by fear of punishment rather than love and gratitude. All of these behaviors look like devotion on the outside, but underneath, they are fueled by anxiety and the impossible pursuit of certainty.

This disorder affects relationships within Christian communities. The struggle with moral OCD can cause people to excessively seek reassurance from pastors, small group leaders, or friends. They repeatedly ask if a particular thought or action was sinful.

Sometimes they avoid serving and ministry out of fear that they will do something wrong, or they might overcommit to prove their faithfulness. Moral OCD creates a version of Christianity that is exhausting, isolating, and disconnected from the grace that God’s word proclaims.

Christian counselors recognize that moral OCD is not a spiritual problem that requires more prayer or greater faith. It is a mental health challenge that requires specific treatment approaches. When these two are confused, a person can experience years of unnecessary suffering, believing they are failing spiritually. In reality, they’re dealing with a diagnosable and treatable condition.

Differentiating Conviction and Compulsion, Certainty and Confidence

For a believer struggling with moral OCD, one of the most difficult aspects is distinguishing between the Holy Spirit’s conviction and the disorder’s compulsions. Conviction from God is typically clear and specific, leading to repentance and peace. This will address actual wrongdoing and point toward restoration.

Conviction is born out of communion, a living relationship with God. Consider receiving feedback from a close friend about your outfit. You may not like what your friend says, but the quality of the relationship allows you to receive it with a sense of peace and safety. You trust your friend’s character, judgment, and care for you. By contrast, you might spend the entire day scrutinizing your appearance and repeatedly adjusting your clothes to satisfy an imagined standard. Yet the goalpost continually shifts, and certainty remains out of reach. The first is rooted in a mutual relationship; the second is the mind curving inward upon itself, searching for a certainty it cannot attain.

Relationships never provide absolute certainty. Instead, they invite confidence in the character of another. You trust that your best friend has your well-being in mind and is not seeking to shame or destroy you. Resting in that confidence, you can move forward with your day without resolving every possible doubt.

In much the same way, moral OCD turns the mind inward in search of absolute moral certainty, whereas genuine faith and conviction grow from reaching outward toward God through God’s Word, God’s Spirit, and God’s people. One traps the person in endless self-examination and leaves them frozen; the other makes room for faithful participation in life, even while uncertainty remains.When people face conviction, it bears the fruit of humility and growth, deepening our relationship with God. Compulsion produces fear and isolation, a sense of unworthiness. Conviction invites us to bring our failures to God and receive forgiveness. But compulsion tells us that we can never be sure we’ve confessed enough, believed enough, or done enough to be acceptable.

This is a vital difference because treating OCD compulsions as if they were a spiritual conviction only strengthens the disorder. Christian counselors understand that both OCD and faith can help individuals learn to recognize these patterns.

Therapy for OCD cannot remove uncertainty by helping clients “figure things out” internally. No amount of analyzing thoughts, feelings, or intentions will produce absolute certainty. Instead, healing comes from helping clients face uncertainty and still act, such as choosing not to check, not to ruminate, or to move forward with life despite doubt. This is the underlying principle of many approaches in treating OCD including Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP).

Scripture reminds us that faith is not about certainty:

By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going. – Hebrews 11:8, NIV

The man whom the apostle Paul called the “father of faith” (Galatians 3:6) did not know where he was going. His pilgrimage was sustained not by certainty, but by a relationship with Almighty God; a relationship in which he learned, slowly and often painfully, to trust. Abraham’s record was far from flawless. His efforts to manufacture security led to much suffering, like fathering Ishmael and twice placing Sarah at risk to protect himself. Yet through these failures, Abraham gradually learned to loosen his grip on control. His journey culminated in the ultimate confrontation with uncertainty: surrendering Isaac to God without knowing how God could possibly fulfill His promise. At that moment, Abraham possessed no certainty about what God would do; he had only a confidence in who God was, a confidence forged through decades of struggle with the goodness and faithfulness of God.

Finding Freedom Through Faith-Informed Treatment

You don’t need to abandon your faith to heal from moral OCD. On the contrary, if moral OCD is a turning inward of the soul to seek certainty, then faith, properly defined and practiced, is precisely the antidote. Finding a Christian counselor who specializes in OCD will help you understand how to honor your beliefs while addressing the disorder with evidence-based treatment.

This type of approach often includes learning to  “turn outward” by being present in the moment and tolerating uncertainty, trusting that God’s love isn’t dependent on achieving perfect certainty about every thought and action.

Consistent with the goal of “turning outward”, community support is important for those who struggle with moral OCD. If a church community understands the struggle, it can respond with compassion rather than judgment. They will learn to recognize that someone seeking constant assurance isn’t lacking faith, but they are dealing with a disorder that requires professional help. These communities can also help by creating environments for mental health treatment is seen as compatible with spiritual growth and not a sign of weakness or insufficient belief.

There Is Hope

Living with moral OCD as a Christian can feel like being trapped between two worlds. You want to follow God faithfully, yet you’re tormented by a disorder that goes against that very desire. There is hope for healing, but it requires that moral OCD be recognized for what it is: a treatable mental health condition.

People can find freedom without abandoning their faith as they learn to distinguish between the voice of fear and the voice of God. Compulsions do not have to override the way they engage in their faith as they discover that the God they have been so afraid of disappointing is the God who says his grace is sufficient.

Moral OCD does not define your faith, and it does not disqualify you from experiencing the fullness of life in Christ. The right support, community, and therapy can open the door to healing. It may be challenging to navigate understanding conviction and compulsion, but it will lead to a faith rooted in grace, not fear.

If you or someone you love is struggling with moral OCD, feel free to contact our office or complete an online contact form. Understanding moral OCD and navigating the journey to healing don’t have to be done alone. Christian counselors are within reach and can help you as you navigate this mental health challenge. Call to learn more.

item.title: Why Traditional Therapies Don’t Always Help Adults with Borderline Autism
item.description:
Have you always felt like there’s something a little different about you, but not different enough for you to know exactly what makes you different? Maybe you’ve done a good job keeping up with the world around you, even though most times you have a harder time fitting in than others.

Maybe you’ve been working hard all your life, socializing, and checking all the boxes, but it still feels like things take more effort than they should. Like social situations leave you completely drained, or unexpected noises, change, or confusion throw you off for hours or even days.

You might have even heard that there’s something called borderline autism in adults, without understanding what it is. This condition is not an official diagnosis, but it does describe real experiences people, much like you, experience every day. People in this group show some traits of autism, but not all, and because of that, traditional therapy may not always be the help you need.

Let’s break down why that happens and what can actually help.

What Borderline Autism in Adults Feels Like

Borderline Autism in Adults exists in a grey area between neurotypical functioning and a clear autism diagnosis. You may not have the signs or mirror the typical idea of someone with autism. In school, you probably did just fine, and socially, you also learned how to copy the behavior of people around you over the years, smiling when you’re supposed to, making small talk, and blending in.

However, after all these years, these seemingly simple social actions have felt harder for you than they look from the outside. Many adults with borderline autism have spent years feeling different without knowing why, having to force themselves to act neurotypical. Unfortunately, these efforts come at a huge cost, causing stress, exhaustion, and identity confusion.

You might not have had a diagnosis growing up, and no one saw what was going on because you didn’t act out. You stayed quiet and always followed the rules. As an adult, you may have been told you have anxiety, ADHD, or depression, and while that may explain some parts, it probably doesn’t explain all of it.

Small Signs That You’re Living with Borderline Autism

There are signs, however, that can help you identify what living with borderline autism might look like. Some of them are:

  • You struggle to follow conversations, especially in groups.
  • You feel uncomfortable in noisy places or crowded rooms.
  • You have a strong need for structure or routine.
  • You stay deeply focused on a specific topic or interest once you’ve started.
  • You deal with big mood swings or getting emotionally stuck over small things.

If you’ve tried therapy before and always left feeling like it didn’t really help, you’re not imagining things. Most mental health approaches are built around standard diagnoses and don’t always work for people with borderline conditions, especially with autism.

This is because traditional therapy usually focuses on fixing you. A lot of therapy is designed to change how you act so you’ll fit in better. Yet if you’re already good at masking, or pretending to be fine when you’re not, this just adds unnecessary pressure. You don’t need fixing, but rather you need support that helps you understand yourself.

Additionally, most social skills training feels unnatural. Some programs teach step-by-step responses for social situations. That might help in a textbook way, but real-life conversations aren’t scripts. If you’ve ever left a conversation feeling like you missed something, even when you said the right things, this might be why.

Likewise, medication isn’t always helpful. Doctors might give you medication for anxiety or mood swings. While that may help with some things, it doesn’t deal with your deeper issues like sensitivity to light, noise, or how exhausting everyday social stuff feels.

Therapies designed for more severe autism cases do not always adapt well to adults with borderline traits. That’s because some of these approaches do not fit the life experiences you deal with daily.

What Life Feels Like Day to Day if You Have Borderline Autism

Borderline autism can leave you socially exhausted. Even a short chat can leave you mentally wiped out. Small talk feels confusing, and group conversations move too fast. You might replay things in your head for hours afterward, trying to figure out what people meant or if you said something wrong.

It can also come with sensory issues. Certain sounds, lights, or fabrics bother you more than they seem to bother others. Maybe just a simple flicker of fluorescent lights, a tag in your clothes, or too many people talking at once can throw you off. These things are hard to explain but easy to feel.

There could also be significant mood crashes. Something small, like an unexpected change in plans or a misunderstanding, can throw your whole day off. You might not always know why you’re feeling down over something others seem to be ok with, but just know it happens.

You probably have one or two things you’re really into. Not in a casual way, but in a way that brings you comfort, focus, or joy. Other people might tell you you’re too into it or not get why you get so focused on it once you start, but it matters to you.

You might be great at your job but still feel unsure when it comes to things others seem to naturally understand, like office politics, vague feedback, or unsaid rules. It’s not that you’re bad at your job; you’re just working twice as hard to understand what others seem to pick up without thinking.

If standard therapy hasn’t worked for you, don’t give up. There are other ways to get support, ways that meet you where you are, not where someone thinks you should be.

Some Therapies That May Help

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy helps you understand and work through unhelpful thoughts, like beating yourself up after social interactions or feeling like a failure when you’re just overstimulated.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy teaches skills for handling big emotions, staying calm during stress, and setting healthy boundaries. It’s especially useful if your emotions feel intense or fast-changing.

Sensory Support involves working with a therapist who understands sensory sensitivities. They can help you slowly build comfort with difficult things, like certain textures or sounds, without pressure.

Creative Therapies include art or music therapy, which give you a way to express yourself without needing to explain everything with words. It can be a break from masking and a way to let your real self breathe.

Occupational Therapy isn’t just for physical rehab; it’s also for creating routines that work with your brain, not against it. It can help with organizing your day, managing time, and building habits that lower stress.

Routine and Adaptive Planning build structure, which is comforting to you. Life isn’t always predictable. Therapy that helps you build routines and also handle change can make a huge difference.

Support for Deep Focus helps you reimagine your ability to hyperfocus. Instead of seeing your intense interests as a problem, some therapists and coaches will help you use them to reach goals, whether that’s through a career, hobby, or creative project.

Support Groups create community with others who also live the same challenges. You don’t have to explain every detail; they just get it, and that alone can lift a huge weight off your shoulders.

You deserve support that fits you, so if other solutions haven’t worked yet for you, it doesn’t mean you’re the problem. It just means you haven’t found the right kind of support yet.

You don’t have to keep pushing through life feeling misunderstood, worn out, or like you’re faking your way through every day. The right help is out there; help that makes sense for how you actually experience the world.

If any part of this sounds familiar, it’s worth talking to someone who can help you find relief. Contact our office today to make an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our association.

item.title: The Trauma of Aging: Where to Find Support
item.description:
Is “trauma” too big a word for this situation? Aging isn’t a dramatic event with alarms, flashing lights, and a solitary life-changing moment. Yet, the evidence of aging in your own life and body can hit harder than you would ever expect. You knew you’d grow old, or at least you hoped you would. But you never knew what aging would actually feel like.

Saying that aging is trauma may not be clinically precise, yet it is emotionally true. Aging is not the trauma of tragedy or catastrophe. It’s natural, normal, and can be anticipated. But those small cumulative losses of independence, stamina, and your youthful good looks can chip away at the self-worth you’ve tried hard to build and maintain.

It feels like trauma

Aging, while natural, can be experienced like a traumatic event for some people. Aging, of course, does not happen in a single moment, but it can still make you feel as if you’ve experienced trauma. It deals with loss, grief, accumulated stress, and unrelenting reminders of your own mortality.

That ongoing exposure to loss and change can feel trauma-like, especially if it triggers anxiety, depression, panic, or reactivates previous trauma such as illness, neglect, abuse, or medical trauma. And it’s more prevalent in cultures that don’t value the aging process, as we see in the modern Western world.

Some therapists might label this as an existential trauma or cumulative trauma rather than a single event. But in strict clinical terms, aging itself is not classified as trauma in the same way that PTSD is defined. True trauma involves a singular or series of traumatic events that involve a threat to life or safety.

But, and this is a big but, your emotions can still feel similar to actual trauma from age-related events. True trauma is often associated with aging, such as medical procedures, loss of a spouse, chronic pain, or serious illness.

This means that aging, while not the singular trauma itself, is often the context in which true trauma can happen. And the process of aging can evoke emotions often associated with trauma because of your personal sense of loss.

I miss my strength and independence

Aging comes with a lot of changes, but these changes aren’t always obvious at first. The gradual loss of strength and stamina can truly alter how you interact with the world around you. What used to come easy, like a long walk or lifting heavy objects, suddenly requires more effort and even forethought. And for many, especially those who value their independence or are known for their physical strength, this is the most difficult age-related adjustment to accept.

But God doesn’t value you for what you can do, what you can lift, or how fast you can do it. In fact, having your own abilities stripped away can also strip away pride. When you can do all things by yourself, you no longer have to rely on God or others. “Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to Him, and He will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6, NIV).

Aging forces you to confront the truth about your body and its limited strength. “Leaning on God” does not just include your own “understanding” but your practical daily needs as well.

This mind shift can push you away from the feelings of loss toward surrendering your own pride. It can teach you gratitude as you learn to rely on family, friends, and community, and yes, to trust God to provide all these things for you. It also teaches patience, as you cannot always take care of your own needs in an instant. It might also teach you empathy for other people in your situation or push you toward asking for forgiveness for past impatient behavior.

I miss my village

With time comes seasons. And seasons change. As you age, not only do you have to deal with your own age-related issues, but you are affected by the changing seasons in others’ lives as well.

Spouses, family members, and lifelong friends pass away. People move after they retire. Adult children become increasingly independent, and you become acutely aware of the shifting dynamics.

You might suddenly feel out of place in a culture that is hyper-fixated on youth. You can no longer relate to the newest trends, and you don’t quite understand all the jokes that everyone else seems to find amusing.

But these circumstances, while they might feel lonely in the moment, are also reminders of the consistency and faithfulness of our never-changing God. The God you knew in your youth, He’s the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8, NIV). And even if you haven’t known God for long, you can be assured that He will never leave you or forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

I Miss My Good Looks

The world is obsessed with youth. Models in magazines have flawless skin and near-perfect physiques. The beauty industry is a multi-billion-dollar business built on the shallow fact that people crave beauty, from themselves and those around them.

So, when you look in the mirror and discover a new gray hair or a wrinkle that has gotten a bit deeper, the emotional impact you feel might feel can hit harder than you know it should.

You know that vanity isn’t a virtue you should be aspiring toward. You probably don’t even want to admit it because it seems so shallow. Yet it can shape how you see yourself and how worthy you feel of love, attention, and belonging.

And when you notice the physical changes in your appearance, it can not only undermine your self-esteem but can be a reminder of the loss of youth, and worse, the progression of aging.

But if you stop and ponder the Word of God, you will realize that maybe you shouldn’t have relied on your looks at all. Maybe this aging process actually weeds out a part of your being that shouldn’t have been there in the first place. That same God is using this process to refine you. Even those gray hairs are tools to draw you closer to the Almighty.

In that way, your focus shifts from what is being taken away from you to what is being revealed and rewarded. 1 Peter 3:3-4 says, “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit which is of great worth in God’s sight” (NIV).

Not only does your aging body help you focus more on what is truly important, your inner self, but it is in itself a reward. “Gray hair is a crown of splendor. It is attained by a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31, NIV).

Therapy

By the time you hit your golden years, you might think that you have everything figured out. You know how to manage your stress reasonably well. You’ve had trauma in your life and survived. But the scars you carry and that underlying, unresolved trauma can cause you to feel anxious, hypervigilant, or angry.

Even if you don’t feel the effects of past trauma, you will likely face new traumas as you age. Medical issues for you and your spouse, transitions such as retirement, moving into elderly care homes, or dealing with other age-related traumas exist.

Christian therapy can help you through these mental and emotional issues and transitions. It can help you understand your body, celebrate your life, and give you hope for a peaceful future. It can help you face your own mortality with acceptance and remove the fear and anxiety surrounding death.

If you’re struggling in the aging process, know that there’s help available to you. At Spokane Christian Counseling, we are here to assist you in overcoming your age-related fear, trauma, and anxiety. Contact our reception team today to help you live more peaceful tomorrows.

item.title: Why the Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women Are Missed During Major Life Changes
item.description:
When people think of bipolar disorder, they imagine mostly crazy mood swings, risky decisions, or extreme behavior. That’s true in many cases, but for many women, the signs can be harder to recognize, especially during big life changes.

The signs of bipolar disorder in women blend into the background of everyday stress, hormonal shifts, responsibilities, and the pressure to keep everything going. This is why mental health challenges like this go unnoticed, particularly during times like pregnancy, postpartum, menopause, or even during job changes or caregiving responsibilities.

Let’s look at why this happens, how it may happen, and what to do when it doesn’t feel quite right to check if bipolar disorder might be a factor.

Why Life Changes Make Things Less Clear

Throughout their lives, women go through major physical and emotional changes. These times naturally bring mood shifts, exhaustion, and irritability. Feeling tired, anxious, or emotionally sensitive after having a baby? That’s normal. Feeling irritable and foggy during menopause? Also normal.

But sometimes, these feelings are more intense than expected, or they come with bursts of energy, racing thoughts, or unexpected behavior.

That’s where things get confusing. Some signs of bipolar disorder in women are quite similar to normal hormonal changes, and they’re often brushed off. A woman might be told she’s just overwhelmed or going through a phase. And while those things may be true, they don’t explain everything.

Think about these examples:

  • A woman who just had a baby hasn’t slept in days. Suddenly, she feels full of energy in the middle of the night and starts reorganizing the house. A few days later, she crashes into sadness she can’t explain. This could actually be more than postpartum blues.
  • Another woman in her late forties starts feeling detached and flat. Then, out of nowhere, she feels jumpy, irritated, and full of restless energy. She may be experiencing a mixed episode.
  • Or a woman with a demanding career goes through phases where she works nonstop, filled with ideas and confidence, only to retreat completely the next week, feeling like she can’t get out of bed. She might be showing real signs of hypomania and depression.

In each case, the emotional ups and downs are real. But so is the possibility of bipolar disorder. And when the two collide, it’s easy to miss what’s really going on.

Why Functional Women Are Overlooked

One of the biggest reasons bipolar disorder goes unnoticed in women is that many of them are still functioning. They’re going to work, caring for kids, managing households, and caring for others. They may even seem more productive than usual during hypomanic phases. When they crash into depression, it’s chalked up to burnout or stress.

Just because someone is still getting things done doesn’t mean they’re feeling okay or mentally well. A few signs that are sometimes ignored in women who seem to be functioning well:

  • Feeling extremely motivated or wired for days, followed by a stretch of low energy or sadness
  • Making decisions on impulse, like sudden purchases, trips, or even quitting a job
  • Talking faster than usual or jumping from one idea to the next
  • Being emotionally sensitive or reactive, without a clear reason
  • Experiencing deep sadness that doesn’t respond to typical coping strategies
  • Having trouble sleeping during energetic phases and oversleeping during low ones

Many of these patterns can be subtle. They don’t always disrupt a woman’s ability to function, but they do affect her relationships, her sense of self, and her long-term mental health.

When Self-Doubt Gets in the Way

Many women live with their symptoms for years without seeking help, not because they’re fine, but because they second-guess themselves. They wonder if they’re just being too emotional, too dramatic, or not strong enough. They blame themselves for not keeping it together or for needing rest when others seem to manage just fine.

This self-doubt is one of the reasons the signs of bipolar disorder in women go unnoticed. Instead of speaking up, women push through. They adjust to the highs and lows, explain them away, and hope things will even out eventually. Some even feel guilty for bringing it up, especially if they’ve already been told it’s just stress or just hormones.

But guilt isn’t a diagnosis, and doubting yourself doesn’t mean you’re imagining things. You know when something feels off. Trusting that feeling is not weakness, it’s wisdom. Being open about your experience doesn’t make you difficult or dramatic. It makes you honest. And honesty is the first step toward support and answers.

In some cases, the signs of bipolar disorder in women are less obvious. They’re woven into personality, habits, or even coping strategies. If you’re wondering whether bipolar disorder might be part of your story, or someone else’s, there are a few less conventional clues to consider.

Other Clues That Don’t Always Get Noticed

  • You’ve been treated for anxiety or depression, but it doesn’t seem to fully explain what you feel. Maybe the medication helps a little, but not enough. Or maybe you’ve always felt like something’s missing from the diagnosis.
  • You feel like there are two versions of yourself. One is full of energy and ideas, the other is tired and disconnected. You swing between them, but you don’t know why.
  • Your moods seem tied to your cycle, seasons, or stress, but the emotional swings feel too strong to be typical. You feel like you’re on a rollercoaster you didn’t sign up for.
  • People say you’re intense or moody, but you’ve always felt like you’re just trying to keep it together. You may have learned to mask your symptoms or push through them, but that doesn’t mean they’re not affecting you.
  • You’ve done things on impulse, like spending sprees or sudden changes, that felt exciting in the moment but later left you confused or regretful.

All of these aren’t things everyone thinks of when they hear bipolar disorder, yet they’re part of what many women experience when living with it. This is especially true for bipolar II or mixed episodes, which are more common in women and harder to recognize.

If any of this sounds familiar, it’s worth exploring further. Bipolar disorder is treatable, but only if it’s properly diagnosed. Many women spend years being treated for depression or anxiety without realizing there’s a deeper pattern underneath it all. And because the signs of bipolar disorder in women aren’t that easy to pick out, it’s important to advocate for yourself, or for someone you love.

What You Can Do Next

  • Start keeping track of your moods, energy levels, and sleep. Even short notes can help spot patterns.
  • Don’t ignore symptoms just because you’re keeping up with daily life. Mental wellness isn’t only about functioning; it’s also about feeling like yourself.
  • Find a mental health professional who understands the signs of bipolar disorder in women.
  • Ask about things like bipolar II or rapid cycling. These are more common in women. They are more subtle but still serious.

If what you’ve read here feels familiar, don’t ignore it. The signs of bipolar disorder in women are real, even if they’ve been misunderstood or overlooked in your life until now. You don’t have to figure this out by yourself, and you don’t have to wait until things get worse to reach out.

Talking to someone who understands women’s mental health, especially during life changes like postpartum, menopause, or times of high stress, can bring a sense of clarity that’s been missing for years. The right support can help you make sense of your moods, your energy, and the parts of yourself that feel unpredictable or exhausting.

You can speak with a licensed Christian counselor who truly listens and understands what you’re facing. Call one of the numbers on your screen or browse the counselors listed on this site to find someone who fits your needs. Whether you’re ready to book a session today or just want to ask a few questions first, someone is here to help.

item.title: How to Keep Your Children from Inheriting Your Trauma
item.description:
Most parents want to give their kids the world, not their trauma. They want to make their life easier, surprise them with much-desired gifts, and set them up for a comfortable and secure future. They want to make sure that their legacy lives on in the lives of their offspring, even after they’re gone. They think about homes, heirlooms, and savings accounts that they’ll someday pass down, assuring their children will get what is rightfully theirs.

This likely sounds like a great undertaking. If we get everything right with no unpredictable events, life will go well for our children. In the real world, this is not possible. Jesus assures us, “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Not everything parents pass down fits into a box or a bank account. In all that focus on giving their kids the best, many parents forget something more important. Parents fail to protect their children from experiencing things like their unresolved pain, old wounds, unhealthy patterns, and harmful parenting practices that are excused because it’s how the parent was raised.

As noble as it is to set your children up for a successful future by giving them monetary gifts, it’s more important to be mindful and self-aware of the internal emotions or activators that cause the parent(s) to react vs. respond to a challenge or struggle. Not passing along negative and detrimental behaviors is critical to decreasing the growth of generational wounds, which decrease the quality of life within the family unit. When parents live in the aftermath of trauma, it changes the way they see the world and how they interact with their children. Poor self-awareness of internal negative thoughts and emotional responses can lead to poor judgment, harming the children, and inadvertently creating trauma for the kids.

Being Raised in the Aftermath of Trauma

Realistically, we can’t eliminate big trauma-inducing events from our lives. You will inevitably face big life moments during your children’s formative years. Death of a loved one, financial struggles, marital issues, health scares, and other difficult moments are bound to happen.

Matthew 5:45 tells us that rain will fall on both the just and the unjust, meaning that no matter how good a person you are, you will face hardships because you’re human and because we are living in a fallen world.

God never promised that He’d remove major obstacles, just that He’d help us walk through and overcome them. As scary and tense as these events might be, they’re not actually what will mentally and emotionally wound your children. What will cause long-lasting negative consequences is your inability to recognize when you are reacting to these traumas.

Trauma, left unprocessed and unhealed, has a way of shaping the way you react vs. respond to stress. Without deliberate and conscious effort, that response is likely to be unhealthy. Stress and trauma aftermath have a way of chipping away at your patience and creating unreasonable fears that can creep into every aspect of your life. Unfortunately, that includes your parenting.

How Trauma Transfers

Children, whether they’re toddlers or teens, look to you as their guidepost and compass. They watch you. They study how you react or respond, and how you cope. And in those moments of crisis when you feel overwhelmed and ready to fall apart, they’re watching.

When you don’t even realize that you’re teaching, you’re showing them how to speak to themselves and how to respond to others, even those who’ve been hostile toward them. You’re showing them how to handle difficult moments, and without even realizing it, they will begin to mirror these actions.

You can also inadvertently transfer your pain and woundedness directly, not just by your example of self-regulation, but by how you treat them during a crisis. Beyond just watching and learning from your example, you’re also molding your child(ren) through your actions.

It’s great if you have composure amid adversity, but sometimes that strength can also make you behave in ways that appear hostile or emotionally unavailable. While you might be handling the crisis itself like a boss, the stress of the situation may appear in more subtle ways. Your tone with them might become sharper or your patience short. You might unconsciously emotionally shut down or place unreasonable expectations on your child.

Though they may seem unrelated and relatively small compared to the big crisis you’re juggling, these subtle but toxic moments can leave a lasting imprint on your child, which may even injure your relationship with them.

How To Interrupt the Transfer

No parent intends to traumatize their child/children. You don’t want to transfer your past or present woundedness to your child, but how do you prevent it? You’ve taken the first step in preventing it by reading this article. By recognizing that trauma can transfer to your child, you are making steps toward preventing it.

How exactly it is transferring may be a little more difficult to decipher because trauma doesn’t always manifest in obvious ways. Yelling or complete emotional withdrawal are easier to identify and control, but subtle trauma responses are often just as damaging.

They show up in patterns such as emotional dysregulation, constant tension, overprotectiveness, emotional unavailability, or inadvertently placing your fears and insecurities onto your child. Children are incredibly perceptive and sense stress incredibly well. They often internalize it even when they don’t verbalize it. Young children are not equipped with the emotional vocabulary to verbalize their feelings, nor are some adults.

To interrupt trauma transfer, ask yourself if you’re reacting out of fear, unresolved anger, grief, or another pain in your past. Am I projecting my anxieties, fears, or overthinking onto my child?

Research shows that children of parents who’ve experienced significant unresolved woundedness, anger, resentment, bitterness, and trauma memories are two to three times more likely to develop anxiety, depression, or PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder). Chronic parental stress can also affect a child’s emotional regulation, alter stress hormone levels, and increase vulnerability to mental health challenges.

The good news is that by recognizing your unresolved trauma responses and identifying negative behavioral patterns in yourself, you can actively work on processing your trauma properly.

Therapy

While you can do some of the work yourself, in trying to identify your negative behavioral patterns and what is triggering (activating) them, it’s wise to employ the help of a professional Christian therapist. In therapy, you can work on resolving your own trauma or the ones that you’ve inherited. You can learn to identify how to become more self-aware of your internal struggles in your thoughts, emotions, and what your body is holding and where it holds it. Identify where you hold anger, anxiety, and bitterness in your body. Seek to grow in self-awareness regarding the responses you’re exhibiting that could be impacting your children.

With the help and guidance of a professional therapist, you can then deal with it. And you can also develop healthier coping mechanisms with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and trauma-focused therapy. You can invite God into the equation, too. Your therapist can point out Scriptures and use biblical principles that can help you interrupt negative and destructive patterns.

By recognizing your responses, the behavior you exhibit in front of your children, and your triggers (those things that cause those behaviors), you can respond intentionally rather than react impulsively. Consistently applying coping strategies will help you break from harmful patterns and give you the skills to create newer, healthier, and more productive ones. You can experience a healthier YOU, a healthier family, more peace and joy, and tools to improve the legacy of your family.

The benefits go way beyond you living a better life. In doing the work now to heal, you are creating a more emotionally safe environment for your children, ensuring they inherit the family heirlooms, not trauma.

God and Trauma

Maybe you inherited old pain and old patterns from long-ago trauma. Maybe you’re still haunted by choices made long before you were born. The Bible doesn’t ignore the fact that trauma can pass from generation to generation. In Exodus 20, God warns of the consequences of sin and brokenness. While they can and often do ripple through families, He promises redemption and healing to those who turn to Him.

This means that while a legacy of pain can affect you, you can heal from it. It also means that it doesn’t have to affect your children and their children. Just as you want to pass down homes, heirlooms, and savings to your children, you also have the power to pass along faith, wisdom, and emotional health.

When you address your own woundedness and lean on God for guidance, you ensure that what you leave behind is a healthy legacy of restoration, redeeming and refreshing the soul. With God, you can create a firm foundation for generations to come.

Learn how to break free from unresolved woundedness and pain through Christian counseling. Contact our reception team today to learn more.

item.title: When Depression Keeps Coming Back: Understanding Depression Cycles in Women
item.description:
Depression doesn’t always arrive with the intention of leaving for good. The hard season begins to feel behind us; the symptoms begin to improve, and then the cloud of depression feels like it has begun to loom over us once again. For women, this return can make the depression cycle exhausting.

Women are more likely than men to experience depression, and out of those women, there is a higher number who will face multiple episodes throughout their lifetime. The first step in finding a sustainable path forward begins with understanding why the depression cycles the way it does.

A woman caught in the cycle of depression feels like she’s slowly losing her footing again after doing all the hard work of showing up to therapy, leaning into faith, and making lifestyle changes. Slowly, the emotional numbness returns, things begin to feel heavy, and everyday life activities feel exhausting. You fight to get out of bed. At that moment, when depression re-enters her life, it can feel more defeating than the first episode.

Why Depression Cycles Back in Women

One thing to understand about recurring depression is that returning to a low season isn’t an indication of failure. Depression is rarely a single event with a clear beginning and a final ending. Many women find that it operates more like a current beneath the surface. It’s manageable for long stretches, then it rises again with a condition shift.

One of the primary drivers of depression cycles in women is hormonal fluctuations. As estrogen and progesterone interact directly with the brain’s mood-regulating systems, there are shifts in these hormones. Women experience shifts in hormones after birth, often experiencing postpartum depression. Then, in her 40s another rapid shift, and a woman may find herself with shifting emotions and experiencing a new depressive episode.

Along with the biological factors, there is relational stress, grief, and seasons of prolonged pressure that can open re-entry points for depression. It is not a cycle that is random, even though it feels that way. When women recognize that there is a pattern beneath this cycling depression, they become empowered in the progress of their healing and mental well-being.

The Emotional Weight of Feeling Like You Keep Starting Over

The first episode of depression carries its own specific grief; the second or third episode carries something heavier. It is a grief that is layered with the loss of progress. One question that often surfaces is “Why do I feel this way again?” It is the distinction of again that matters.

A history of depressive episodes is one of the strongest predictors of future ones. This indicates that having walked through depression before may increase vulnerability to experiencing those depression cycles again.

The reality is deeply unfair for a woman who fought her way to a better season. She feels and believes that she deserves to stay there, but when depression arrives, she becomes burdened with grief that goes beyond sadness and closer to despair. God does not look away from women who find themselves immersed in this kind of grief. The Psalms are full of honest cries from people who have felt like they were in the same dark place.

David wrote repeatedly of his soul being downcast and crying out while feeling unheard. But it also speaks of David returning to the reminder that God and His steadfast love do not change (Psalm 42:11). This pattern of honest lament, when paired with stubborn hope, can give women caught in a depression cycle something real to hold onto. They are never disqualified from God’s care.

Shame and the Depression Cycle

The shame that accumulates around recurring depression is one of the least discussed dimensions of this cycle. One single episode of depression can carry stigma, but when it returns – again and again – women begin to internalize a story that there is something fundamentally wrong with them. They can question if their faith is strong enough or if they have tried hard enough. They feel as though healing is just beyond their reach, and that thought intensifies the shame.

Shame will actively work against any behavior that is help-seeking. It will drive people inward as it pulls them from support systems that could help interrupt the cycle. Women of faith find this especially layered. The belief that God heals sometimes quietly becomes a source of guilt when depression persists. If healing is possible, and she is not healed, then the internal logic concludes that the problem is her. This is not the truth that is found in God’s word.

Christian counselors who work with women experiencing depression cycles are trying to untangle this distorted thinking. They work to help women separate the clinical reality of a mood disorder from the spiritual identity of the person experiencing it. Depression is not a character flaw, and when it returns, it is not evidence of a spiritual weakness. When women name that distinction out loud in a safe space, the shame grip loosens as the cycle begins to slow.

Finding Steadier Ground Through Pattern and Support

Breaking the pattern of a depression cycle doesn’t always mean that it will stop entirely. The more realistic and meaningful goal of breaking this pattern is to recognize it sooner, respond to it quicker, and recover with less distance.

Tracing mood patterns alongside hormone changes, sleep quality, stress, and seasonal shifts is a practical tool that will help women identify personal triggers. When a woman can see her own pattern clearly, she can move from feeling ambushed by depression to feeling partially prepared for it. This preparation changes the internal experience.

Working through patterns and support, Christian counselors can bring an approach that will be integrated to hold space for the clinical and spiritual dimensions of a woman’s unique experience. They understand that a woman who is grappling with recurring depression may need practical coping tools, as well as conversations about faith, identity, and what it means to be held by God.

The book of Lamentations was written in the aftermath of an enormous loss and devastation. It contains one of the most enduring reminders of God’s new mercies every morning. It reassures women that his faithfulness does not waver, even when everything else feels broken. (Lamentations 3:22-23). When a woman is in the middle of a depressive cycle, this is an anchor that will hold true while the work of healing continues.

Finding Your Way Back, One Season at a Time

A depression cycle does not indicate that healing is impossible. It is a sign that depression is a condition for many women that requires ongoing attention rather than one single intervention. The woman who finds herself in another low season is not back at the beginning. Because of what she has already learned, she carries wisdom regarding the cycle, even though it does not feel that way.

A woman having a history of depression may mean having another occurrence during her lifetime, but it does not mean a lack of hope or make her a liability. Often, with the right support, the depression becomes easier to navigate, and knowledge is gained.

If you are a woman who feels discouraged or has become isolated because of a depression cycle, you don’t have to remain in that space alone. Reaching out for support is a meaningful step that can remove spiritual confusion and open the doorway to strength and healing.

Take time to contact our office and speak with our reception team. They are available to answer questions, connect you with the right support, and start navigating the pathway to overcoming the cycles of depression.

You will find the information and tools that will help you work through the recurring depression as you stay grounded in your faith. The goal is learning to come back to steadiness with greater skill, greater compassion, and a stronger faith in the hard seasons.

item.title: The Real Reason You Constantly Feel Guilty
item.description:
Some people go through their entire lives feeling guilty, without ever feeling as if they can atone for their mistakes or be fully forgiven and accepted. Guilt can be a helpful response to something. When you make a mistake, your moral compass tries to steer you back to your values with a sense of guilt and shame. Usually, these emotions are resolved when you make things right.

When guilt and shame persist for years, that’s a sign that something is stuck. Guilt that persists for years and decades, however, is not a prolonged attack of conscience. Feelings of constant guilt are your body’s default way of trying to keep you safe. You can resolve persistent guilt, but it will require you to be vulnerable with someone.

Your Conscience as Your Guide

To understand why you constantly feel guilty, you must understand what appropriate guilt looks and feels like, and then compare it with your experience of feeling guilty. Appropriate guilt doesn’t persist for years or decades. It is an immediate cognitive response that acts as a motivator to change the situation, and usually it is clearly connected with wrongdoing.

Let’s say that there is a coworker whom you dislike. One day, you are talking about this coworker with another friend at work, saying unkind things about them and laughing cruelly. You discover that they have walked into the room behind you and have heard you mocking them. Even though you dislike them, you will still likely feel terrible about having been caught in the act of being mean about them.

In a scenario like this, guilt is a response to being caught behaving badly. It is appropriate and will likely motivate you to apologize and perhaps even amend your working relationship with this person.

Appropriate guilt is a logical response to wrongdoing. Once you have done the work to resolve the issue and make amends, that guilty feeling should subside and make way for other emotions like relief, gratitude, and determination to avoid further wrongdoing. In this way, it’s a helpful emotion. What happens when you can’t stop feeling guilty, though?

A Frozen Nervous System

You can’t think yourself out of feeling guilty, and positive affirmations can’t make you feel better. This is because persistent guilt is not an emotion you need to process, nor is it a thought you need to challenge. Constant guilt is a sign that you don’t feel emotionally safe.

In the example of being caught gossiping about your coworker, you had a physical response to being caught in the middle of wrongdoing. In that moment, you were suddenly unsafe because one of your flaws was exposed. That might have affected your reputation in the workplace, your friend’s reputation, or even your job itself. Guilt motivated you to take action by apologizing, so that you could feel safe again.

Persistent guilt and shame often stem from childhood experiences of constantly being criticized, and it is often attached to conditions like OCD, trauma, depression, and perfectionism. It might be stored in your mind as memories or a harsh inner voice constantly criticizing you. It cannot be resolved in your thoughts alone. Persistent guilt is stored in your body, and the only way it can be resolved is to feel safe, seen, accepted, understood, and loved.

The Fig Leaf

In the book of Genesis, we are told that Adam and Eve’s first actions after eating the forbidden fruit were to make fig leaf coverings to hide their nakedness. After that, they hid when God came looking for them. Guilt always combines with shame. This causes us to cover up and hide ourselves away from connection and relationships, especially with those who know us best.

Covering up or isolating yourself will not help. This is not how we feel safe. If anything, isolating yourself will make you feel less safe as you cut off your much-needed emotional support.

You might constantly feel guilty because you were told throughout childhood that there was something flawed about you. Your parents might have been your first bullies, and you have been covering up your authentic self for decades. When you mask important parts of yourself like this, others can’t see you, accept you, or validate you.

You might feel guilty because you do not allow yourself to be seen by others. The only way you will stop feeling guilty all the time is when you are exposed and vulnerable to someone. You need to allow them to validate and love you for being exactly who you are.

Your nervous system will only come out of panic mode, and your guilt will only be resolved, when you can be vulnerable with someone who remains steady and shows you complete acceptance. Only then will you be able to drop your defenses and pretenses, stop performing or trying to earn love, and accept your flaws.

When this happens, your nervous system learns that it is possible to feel safe, possibly for the first time. You’re not perfect; you will make mistakes in the future, but you don’t have to be perfect to be seen, accepted, and loved. This is what safety feels like.

Signs You’re Moving Away from Constantly Feeling Guilty

When you feel safe, you don’t have to continue monitoring yourself, masking your behavior, or keeping your opinions to yourself. You can express your thoughts and state your preferences. You don’t have to hide behind a carefully constructed mask of politeness and peacekeeping. It’s not about acting out-of-character; this is you being your authentic self.

One of the signs that you are resolving your guilt is that you stop apologizing. Before, you were likely apologizing for everything, even when you were doing nothing wrong. When you’re not feeling guilty all the time, you will stop apologizing as if everything is always your fault.

On the other hand, without persistent guilt, you can take accountability for your mistakes and own up to your failures. Sometimes, persistent guilt causes you to cover up your mistakes or gaslight your way out of issues. When you can feel appropriate guilt for your wrongs, you can make amends whenever necessary, without your feelings getting overwhelmed by the incident.

Most importantly, you will know that you have left persistent guilt behind when that harsh inner critic is finally silenced. Perhaps it was an echo of your mother or father’s voice, always criticizing, demeaning, and mocking your every action. Maybe it was your own voice telling you that you were constantly getting things wrong.

When you have stopped feeling guilty all the time, you will only hear that voice occasionally, and usually only when you have done something that can be resolved. Even better than the inner critic voice being silenced, however, is when you begin hearing a small whisper that tells you, “Good job,” “Well done,” and “You deserve good things.”

You may have carried guilt and shame for the longest time, without knowing why and without knowing how to be free. You don’t have to continue like this, but you can’t go on alone. When you meet someone who keeps calm, steady, and accepting when you are vulnerable, you will find the guilt fades. There are people in the world who want to see you, validate you, and love you.

When you go for counseling, you get to be yourself with someone who will never judge you. For many people, this is the first time they have ever felt seen, understood, and validated. If you would like to begin meeting with a counselor, we can help. Please consult our online catalog or speak with our reception team to find someone who can help you overcome persistent guilt.
