item.title: The Benefits of Sleep and Why We Need It
item.description:
Studies have found that the benefits of sleep go beyond just giving your body and brain a rest from the stimuli and rigors of the day. It is a biological necessity. Certain processes vital to your health and well-being can only happen when your body powers down and you are asleep.

It is a common experience that a problem difficult at night is resolved in the morning after the committee of sleep has worked on it. – John Steinbeck

Sleep supports brain function, physical recovery, and immune system function by providing a period of quietness. This is one of the biggest benefits of sleep. It enables the brain to reset and restore its connections and carry out important processes. These involve memory consolidation, hormone regulation, tissue repair, and the restoration of energy.

Without enough quality sleep, your body and brain are unable to function properly. This can affect your mood and emotional well-being, concentration, judgment, reaction time, and ability to think clearly. It can also increase the risk of chronic health problems such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

How Sleep Works

Sleep is an active process that consists of four distinct stages that a healthy person cycles through multiple times during the night. Each stage plays an essential part in the cycle that enables your brain and body to recover and grow. This helps you wake up refreshed and ready to face the day ahead.

Stage 1 (N1): N1 is the first and lightest stage of sleep and is easy to wake up from. It is a dozing off, transition period that only happens when you first fall asleep, and typically lasts just a few minutes. During this phase, heartbeat and breathing start to slow, muscles relax, and you may experience occasional sensations of falling as you start to nod off.

Stage 2 (N2): N2 is the longest sleep stage, making up roughly 45-55% of your total sleep time. It is a light to moderate phase during which your body temperature drops, muscles relax more deeply, heart rate and breathing slow, eye movement stops, and brain waves slow down. The brain has short bursts of activity that some researchers believe happen as it reorganizes memories and information gleaned while you were awake.

Stage 3 (N3): N3, also known as deep, slow-wave, or delta sleep, is the deepest sleep stage. Your body is the most relaxed during this stage, and it is the hardest one to wake up from. This is the restorative phase of sleep.

During N3, growth and other hormones critical to the repair and rebuilding of your body and mind are released into your bloodstream, strengthening your immune system and enabling tissue repair as your body heals and grows. Even though brain activity is reduced during this stage, some studies show that deep, delta wave sleep contributes to creativity, insightful thinking, and memory.

Stage 4 (REM Sleep): REM sleep is where most dreaming takes place. Brain activity increases to close to what it is when you are awake. Your eyes move rapidly behind your eyelids, and voluntary muscles such as your arms, legs, and torso become temporarily immobilized. This is to protect you from physically acting out vivid dreams and potentially injuring yourself.

During the night, you may go through several sleep cycles. Most typically, people go through four to six of them. Not all are the same length, but on average, they tend to last about 90 minutes.

Benefits of Sleep

In addition to boosting your energy and alertness by providing you with an extended period of stillness and reduced activity, sleep enables several essential physical and psychological functions to take place that cannot happen in the body’s awake state.

Restoration and Repair: During sleep, the brain clears out waste products and neurotoxins that accumulate throughout the day. It also releases hormones necessary for body tissues to be able to grow and repair themselves.

Improved Executive Function: Healthy sleep improves executive functions such as sound judgment and decision-making. It improves your ability to recognize and react appropriately to danger and threats.

Problem-Solving: As neurotoxins are cleared from the brain during sleep, cognitive functions such as logical reasoning are enhanced. Studies have shown that when facing a complicated problem, sleep often improves your chances of finding a creative solution to it when you wake up.

Memory Consolidation: Sleep enables the brain to organize, categorize, and consolidate memories and learned information so they take root. This boosts memory and makes it easier to access and use things you learn, increases attention span, and improves focus and concentration.

Emotional Regulation: Sleep reduces irritability and anxiety, improves your mood, and helps you regulate your emotions. This occurs by enabling you to better handle the physical and emotional effects of stress.

Strengthened Immune System: Adequate sleep strengthens immune function, enhances your immune system’s ability to identify potential threats, and increases your body’s ability to fight off disease and infections.

Improved Heart Health and Reduced Inflammation: Sleep slows down your heart rate, lowers blood pressure, reduces inflammation, and decreases your risk of stroke or cardiovascular disease.

Improved Metabolism: Getting enough sleep helps improve your metabolism, which promotes blood sugar control, reduces the risk of diabetes, and helps you maintain a healthy weight.

Enhances Athletic Performance: Adequate sleep facilitates tissue repair, cell regeneration, and muscle growth, and contributes to enhanced endurance, alertness, and response time.

Effects of Sleep Deprivation

Sleep deprivation can affect your mood, reduce your ability to control your emotions, impair your judgment, and hurt your mental health and physical well-being.

In addition to causing you to feel tired or sluggish during the day, insufficient sleep makes it harder to focus, think clearly, or remember information. It also decreases your attention span and ability to make sound decisions. A lack of sleep can lead to cloudy thinking that heightens your risk of making costly mistakes or becoming involved in an accident.

If allowed to become persistent and long-term, sleep deprivation can weaken your immune system. This can increase your susceptibility to sickness and chronic health issues such as cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Extended sleep deprivation can also interfere with your metabolism, cause relationships to suffer, lead to depression and anxiety, and even shorten your life.

Tips for Getting a Good Night’s Sleep

  • Create and commit to a regular sleep schedule to help your body maintain a consistent internal clock.
  • Adopt a relaxing bedtime routine that helps you wind down before bed and make it easier to fall asleep.
  • As much as possible, go to bed and get up at the same time every day – even on weekends or when on vacation.
  • Make your bedroom a comfortable, relaxing, soothing place, and keep it cool, dark, and quiet.
  • Stop using electronics and avoid screen time at least an hour before bed.
  • Store digital devices somewhere other than your bedroom.
  • Keep naps short, and avoid napping late in the day.
  • Get exposure to at least 20 minutes of natural light first thing in the morning.
  • Exercise regularly, preferably early in the day.
  • Avoid late-night snacking.
  • Avoid using alcohol, nicotine, or caffeine late in the day or before bed.
  • If you can’t fall asleep, don’t try to force it. Instead, try picking up a book and reading until you start to feel sleepy.

Benefits of Sleep Therapy

If you have been having trouble falling or staying asleep and getting the rest you need, you may want to consider sleep therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), in particular, is an effective non-drug treatment that addresses the root causes of your struggles with sleep rather than just the symptoms.

CBT-I helps you identify negative thought patterns and behaviors that may be contributing to your difficulties and retrain your brain to replace them with new ones that support better sleep. This can be explored with a trained therapist like those in this office.

If you would like to set up an appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors at our location, please give us a call. Your first appointment is risk-free.

References:
Eric Suni. “Stages of Sleep: What Happens in a Normal Sleep Cycle?” Sleep Foundation. Updated July 25, 2025. sleepfoundation.org/stages-of-sleep.
Lucy Bryan. “Why Is Sleep Important?” Sleep Foundation. Updated June 11, 2026. sleepfoundation.org/how-sleep-works/why-do-we-need-sleep.

Photos:
“Sleeping Man”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; “Naptime”, Courtesy of Andredj Lišakov, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post The Benefits of Sleep and Why We Need It appeared first on Mill Creek Christian Counseling.

item.title: Managing Attention and Hyperactivity Deficits with Counseling
item.description:
Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder, where a person has difficulty concentrating to the point of completing tasks, or impulsivity, a type of driven restlessness to a degree that it impacts all areas of life, is not a newly noted pattern in human behavior.

The description has shown up in literature in different ways throughout recent history, and most likely will change again over time as more is discovered about where it comes from and how it appears or presents itself in cultures over time (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). There certainly has been a lot of progress in tracking and understanding the description of behaviors.

There are also now numerous, effective, researched ways to understand and manage the symptoms, all of which should be, when in relationship with God, wrestled with and considered before Him. Understanding can begin by meeting with your doctor or a psychologist or therapist to assess whether your symptoms meet the criteria for the diagnosis.

Then, as with all things in making decisions, including mental health diagnosis and its treatment, we are invited to pray, review Scripture for guidance, and seek wise counsel to learn to manage ourselves.

In the written encouragement from E. Welch (2024), “The most important principle is that your quest for medical treatment does not outdistance your diligence in spiritual nurture.” Counseling with a mental health professional, grounded in Christ and biblical truths, can be one way to explore and develop understanding and skills to manage ADHD.

What is ADHD?

Before describing ADHD, there needs to be a discussion of the importance of the descriptors themselves. Frustration has been expressed at the ways in which terms for the same behavior or descriptors change over time. Does what we call something really matter? The pendulum may swing, but we must let it land where the Lord directs. We are directed to be thoughtful of how our words affect others.

As Proverbs 18:21 (CSB) says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue….” Additionally, we are directed to be mindful of what we say, as it reflects our hearts, and mindful of how our words will impact others and the situations we are in (cf. Proverbs 10:19).

Additionally, the euphemism, “I just don’t have the words,” exists for a reason. Language can fall short of describing what we see and know. Ultimately, what we say matters in our own heads to ourselves and toward others. Bearing that in mind, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is one description of a set of patterns of behaviors. It is not a newly recognized nuance in human behavior.

Descriptions of inattention first appeared in literature in 1798 by Sir Alexander Crichton, where he explored what might be typical versus atypical patterns of attention (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). Centuries later, ADHD is described by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM-5-TR) as a combination of six or more specific symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity, or both.

They must be present for more than six months, having started before the age of twelve, and significantly impact more than two areas of life in ways that negatively impact the person and are not consistent with what are considered developmental averages.

What medical or mental health providers are looking for is how attention and activity show up and impact living. Consider that a person with attention-deficit can attend and concentrate highly on a singular task, usually something of great interest to them, which is usually not the task at hand or required in their setting.

Attention is rapidly pulled to multiple places, like someone changing the TV channel multiple times without consent (Copeland and Dumm, 2015). It is physiologically and often emotionally exhausting, and this is where behavior starts to affect functioning in different settings.

Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019) calls this “The GAP.” Hyperactivity is a type of driven restlessness, like an overheated internal motor that is either set to max RPMs at all times, looking for ways to release the vibrating energy, or turned completely off. ADHD is essentially not about a person’s ability, but a person’s performance.

When diagnosing ADHD, it is important that symptoms are differentiated from what is simply healthy play or activities for children and adults. An assessment also should consider a person’s personality, their environment, stressors, and medical implications that may present like ADHD, but are not actually its cause.

ADHD needs to be assessed, and other diagnoses that impact cognition and brain functioning need to be considered; things like learning disabilities, possible traumatic brain injuries, substances, etc. (Welch, 2024).

Where ADHD Comes From

There is still much to learn about ADHD and its development. Even research appears to disagree with itself, where some studies state that there is no concrete evidence that ADHD brain development and functioning are different from other neurotypical brains (Welch, 2024). Other research points to evidence that there is indeed neurodivergence in someone who has ADHD (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

What is known is that some factors increase the likelihood of ADHD behaviors recurring, such as heritability (where parents had the official diagnosis or presented with similar behaviors), children with low birth weight, infants and children exposed to nicotine and alcohol, and chemical changes that occur from extreme stress occurring from different factors in parents.

Studies of people with an ADHD diagnosis show a thinner cortex, more activity in the occipital lobe, the back of the brain, which impacts visual learning, and less activity in the frontal and temporal lobes where sequencing and decision-making occur (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

When is it really inattention and hyperactivity disorder?

As every person has their own unique summary of genetics and experiences, ADHD may look different in how it shows up from day to day. Therefore, it is essential that when managing ADHD, diagnosing ADHD, or relating to someone with ADHD, you get to know yourself or that person to figure out where the performance GAPS exist and why, and over time. Again, ADHD is not about a person’s intelligence; it is about performance.

The criteria for assessment are important in this, assessing the way symptoms show up across different environments and from a young age. For example, a parent expresses their concern that their child will make eye contact briefly but then act as if the connection was not made and begin behaving beyond or outside of what they were requested to do. This may fall under the category of difficulty sustaining attention.

In order to assess whether this is part of ADHD, an assessment needs to evaluate multiple factors to identify why this behavior occurs in daily life. Questions should be explored, such as whether the child may have hearing or vision impairment that may be impacting connection.

Is there a cultural layer at play where direct or sustained eye contact with a parent is acceptable? When, where, and how is the child being required to provide sustained attention? Is the environment chaotic or peaceful in these contexts? Is the concern only happening with one parent, or with all people? Is the child’s personality assertive or more passive? Did the child just eat, and maybe mood fluctuation is playing a role?

There are many ways and reasons divergence appears in daily life, but what is imperative is careful and thoughtful consideration of why it is impacting progress or daily functioning.

Using Counseling to Manage ADHD

As noted previously, the first step to diagnosing and managing ADHD is to pray about it. Set a rhythm of bringing thoughts and curiosities to God and anticipating that He will respond in expected and unexpected ways. This may be through Scripture, through exploration of literature on the subject, through others with wise advice and encouragement, and through counseling.

In addition, consider scheduling multiple appointments to meet with a primary care physician, a psychologist, and a therapist to have symptoms assessed. Consider their feedback and whether there is a pattern that illuminates what might be occurring. Ongoing counseling, regardless of the outcomes from a doctor and psychologist, can be beneficial in addressing what problems may be arising that led to an assessment of symptoms in the first place.

A counselor can help be a resource or director of increasing self-awareness and education about symptoms. They could provide literature and self-help tools to begin managing symptoms. Counselors can adjust session times, styles, and treatment interventions to help develop self-management tools and skills.

For some people with ADHD, medication is part of their management tools, and counseling can be a good place to process the feelings and integration of medication after seeing their doctor or psychiatrist for the actual prescription of medication. A counselor can become the one person who works to understand their experience, identify the differences in their experience, provide direction, and walk alongside with compassion.

Lastly, a counselor rooted in Christ and biblical faith can help illuminate how to practically implement God’s encouragement to all of us to have rhythms that reflect him, or filter life through Christ, no matter how our brains operate or our bodies move.

Copeland, L. A. (2015). Hunter And His Amazing Remote (B. Dumm, Illus.). Amazon.
Lange KW, Reichl S, Lange KM, Tucha L, Tucha O. “The History of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.” Atten Defic Hyperact Disord. 2010 Dec;2(4):241-55. doi: 10.1007/s12402-010-0045-8. Epub 2010 Nov 30. PMID: 21258430; PMCID: PMC3000907.
Welch, E. T. (2024). Blame It on The Brain? Distinguishing Chemical Imbalances, Brain Disorders, and Disobedience (2nd ed.). P&R Publishing.

item.title: Managing Attention and Hyperactivity Deficits with Counseling
item.description:
Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder, where a person has difficulty concentrating to the point of completing tasks, or impulsivity, a type of driven restlessness to a degree that it impacts all areas of life, is not a newly noted pattern in human behavior.

The description has shown up in literature in different ways throughout recent history, and most likely will change again over time as more is discovered about where it comes from and how it appears or presents itself in cultures over time (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). There certainly has been a lot of progress in tracking and understanding the description of behaviors.

There are also now numerous, effective, researched ways to understand and manage the symptoms, all of which should be, when in relationship with God, wrestled with and considered before Him. Understanding can begin by meeting with your doctor or a psychologist or therapist to assess whether your symptoms meet the criteria for the diagnosis.

Then, as with all things in making decisions, including mental health diagnosis and its treatment, we are invited to pray, review Scripture for guidance, and seek wise counsel to learn to manage ourselves.

In the written encouragement from E. Welch (2024), “The most important principle is that your quest for medical treatment does not outdistance your diligence in spiritual nurture.” Counseling with a mental health professional, grounded in Christ and biblical truths, can be one way to explore and develop understanding and skills to manage ADHD.

What is ADHD?

Before describing ADHD, there needs to be a discussion of the importance of the descriptors themselves. Frustration has been expressed at the ways in which terms for the same behavior or descriptors change over time. Does what we call something really matter? The pendulum may swing, but we must let it land where the Lord directs. We are directed to be thoughtful of how our words affect others.

As Proverbs 18:21 (CSB) says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue….” Additionally, we are directed to be mindful of what we say, as it reflects our hearts, and mindful of how our words will impact others and the situations we are in (cf. Proverbs 10:19).

Additionally, the euphemism, “I just don’t have the words,” exists for a reason. Language can fall short of describing what we see and know. Ultimately, what we say matters in our own heads to ourselves and toward others. Bearing that in mind, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is one description of a set of patterns of behaviors. It is not a newly recognized nuance in human behavior.

Descriptions of inattention first appeared in literature in 1798 by Sir Alexander Crichton, where he explored what might be typical versus atypical patterns of attention (Lange K.W. Et al., 2010). Centuries later, ADHD is described by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM-5-TR) as a combination of six or more specific symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity, or both.

They must be present for more than six months, having started before the age of twelve, and significantly impact more than two areas of life in ways that negatively impact the person and are not consistent with what are considered developmental averages.

What medical or mental health providers are looking for is how attention and activity show up and impact living. Consider that a person with attention-deficit can attend and concentrate highly on a singular task, usually something of great interest to them, which is usually not the task at hand or required in their setting.

Attention is rapidly pulled to multiple places, like someone changing the TV channel multiple times without consent (Copeland and Dumm, 2015). It is physiologically and often emotionally exhausting, and this is where behavior starts to affect functioning in different settings.

Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019) calls this “The GAP.” Hyperactivity is a type of driven restlessness, like an overheated internal motor that is either set to max RPMs at all times, looking for ways to release the vibrating energy, or turned completely off. ADHD is essentially not about a person’s ability, but a person’s performance.

When diagnosing ADHD, it is important that symptoms are differentiated from what is simply healthy play or activities for children and adults. An assessment also should consider a person’s personality, their environment, stressors, and medical implications that may present like ADHD, but are not actually its cause.

ADHD needs to be assessed, and other diagnoses that impact cognition and brain functioning need to be considered; things like learning disabilities, possible traumatic brain injuries, substances, etc. (Welch, 2024).

Where ADHD Comes From

There is still much to learn about ADHD and its development. Even research appears to disagree with itself, where some studies state that there is no concrete evidence that ADHD brain development and functioning are different from other neurotypical brains (Welch, 2024). Other research points to evidence that there is indeed neurodivergence in someone who has ADHD (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

What is known is that some factors increase the likelihood of ADHD behaviors recurring, such as heritability (where parents had the official diagnosis or presented with similar behaviors), children with low birth weight, infants and children exposed to nicotine and alcohol, and chemical changes that occur from extreme stress occurring from different factors in parents.

Studies of people with an ADHD diagnosis show a thinner cortex, more activity in the occipital lobe, the back of the brain, which impacts visual learning, and less activity in the frontal and temporal lobes where sequencing and decision-making occur (Nowell, David, Ph.D. (2019, February).

When is it really inattention and hyperactivity disorder?

As every person has their own unique summary of genetics and experiences, ADHD may look different in how it shows up from day to day. Therefore, it is essential that when managing ADHD, diagnosing ADHD, or relating to someone with ADHD, you get to know yourself or that person to figure out where the performance GAPS exist and why, and over time. Again, ADHD is not about a person’s intelligence; it is about performance.

The criteria for assessment are important in this, assessing the way symptoms show up across different environments and from a young age. For example, a parent expresses their concern that their child will make eye contact briefly but then act as if the connection was not made and begin behaving beyond or outside of what they were requested to do. This may fall under the category of difficulty sustaining attention.

In order to assess whether this is part of ADHD, an assessment needs to evaluate multiple factors to identify why this behavior occurs in daily life. Questions should be explored, such as whether the child may have hearing or vision impairment that may be impacting connection.

Is there a cultural layer at play where direct or sustained eye contact with a parent is acceptable? When, where, and how is the child being required to provide sustained attention? Did the child just eat, and maybe mood fluctuation is playing a role?

As noted previously, the first step to diagnosing and managing ADHD is to pray about it. In addition, consider scheduling multiple appointments to meet with a primary care physician, a psychologist, and a therapist to have symptoms assessed. Consider their feedback and whether there is a pattern that illuminates what might be occurring. A counselor can help be a resource or director of increasing self-awareness and education about symptoms. They could provide literature and self-help tools to begin managing symptoms. For some people with ADHD, medication is part of their management tools, and counseling can be a good place to process the feelings and integration of medication after seeing their doctor or psychiatrist for the actual prescription of medication. Copeland, L. A. (2015). Hunter And His Amazing Remote (B. Dumm, Illus.). Amazon.
Lange KW, Reichl S, Lange KM, Tucha L, Tucha O. “The History of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.” Atten Defic Hyperact Disord. 2010 Dec;2(4):241-55. doi: 10.1007/s12402-010-0045-8. Epub 2010 Nov 30. PMID: 21258430; PMCID: PMC3000907.

item.title: What Depression Feels Like and How It Affects Your Life
item.description:
Every year, approximately 21 million adults and 4 million adolescents in the United States experience at least one major depressive episode. There are likely more people who have struggled with their mental health in the last twelve months but who did not reach out for support or contribute to these statistics. Many of us do not truly know what depression feels like, how to deal with it, or when to get support.

All forms of depression are treatable with a combination of therapy, medication, and changes to your lifestyle. However, before you attempt to treat depression, you must first identify it. Once you have learned what depression feels like, you will be better equipped to handle it.

What Depression Feels Like

Your mind, body, and emotions are all connected and constantly affect each other, whether you realize it or not. For example, you will feel a physical illness in your body with symptoms like elevated temperature, difficulty breathing, or sore muscles, but the same sickness also affects your mood. Emotionally, you will feel more subdued, more in need of intimacy with others, and even a little hopeless. What is happening on the outside affects how you feel on the inside.

Sometimes the opposite is true; your emotions reflect in physical sensations and actions. When you are joyful, you might sing or whistle as you do certain tasks. When you are anxious, you might feel sweaty, and your muscles will tense in readiness for action. When you are disappointed, your shoulders tend to slump, your head feels heavier than normal, and you might struggle to make eye contact with others.

You can learn to identify what depression feels like, even though it is not a single emotion. You experience many different emotions during depression and feel various physical sensations. Depression affects your body, mindset, and mood. Over time, your habits, routine, and overall way of life can also be affected.

You might wonder why you are constantly tired, emotionally numb, and never in the mood to see your friends anymore. You could try treating these symptoms individually, but your diminished energy and motivation may significantly inhibit making a change.

People experience depression for multiple reasons. These could be things like grief, chemical imbalances in the brain, exhaustion from overwork, or mood disorders. To treat depression, we often begin by noticing the symptoms and then working back to the possible sources.

The best thing you can do for yourself is to be honest about what you’re experiencing and to speak with someone about it. If you have noticed any of the following changes in your life, consider reaching out to a loved one or professional for further support.

Increased Irritability and Anger

Anger, frustration, and irritability are often precursors or companions to depression. It is most noticeable in people who rarely lose their temper or show anger. If you are suddenly brooding and short-tempered, feeling impatient with everything and everyone, you might be battling depression.

Being in a constantly irritable mood will affect those who interact with you daily. Loved ones, acquaintances, and work colleagues will question you. At times you will deeply regret lashing out or losing your temper, but feel helpless to do anything other. You might benefit from anger management, or perhaps you have depression over an issue that needs addressing.

Changes to Your Appetite

Did you know that your eating habits often reflect your mental health? If there has been a recent change to your appetite with no medical explanation, this is often an indicator of what depression feels like. You might have an increased appetite, especially for sugary, salty, fatty food. These foods trigger dopamine production and can make you feel better emotionally, but only for a moment.

On the other hand, you might have a drastically decreased appetite, with no energy even for fast food. It’s not simply that you feel unmotivated to cook and clean up after yourself, but even eating feels like it would be a chore that you have no energy for. Unfortunately, this has a domino effect where your appetite leads to decreased energy, contributing to an even lower mood.

Constant Fatigue and Inactivity

Depression drains you of all enthusiasm and energy. One aspect of this is the dietary changes, causing you to have fewer nutrients and less energy. Another common aspect of depression-related fatigue is feeling overly anxious about the state of your physical health, but not having the motivation to do anything about it.

This sinks you lower into feelings of self-consciousness, self-loathing, and dramatically reduced self-esteem. As you begin to consider the tasks you have fallen behind in, you become so overwhelmed that, once again, you cannot find the energy or motivation to make the changes. It’s a cycle that can feel hard to escape.

Isolation

When you wonder what depression feels like, most commonly it feels like wanting to hide away from the world. So many of the habits we form when depressed are self-sabotaging. We need a better diet, some good sleep, some physical activity, and some friends around us, but we avoid these things and end up sinking even lower.

You avoid your friends and loved ones when you are depressed because you don’t want to burden them. Sometimes you can’t articulate or explain what you’re going through, and so it’s easier not even to try.

You might have friends who would confront or challenge you simply from seeing your appearance, and you’d rather not face it. Isolation feels protective, but it always makes things far worse. You need support, community, loved ones, and someone who will listen well.

Worsening Hygiene

At some point, you may have such a lack of motivation and energy that you stop caring for yourself practically. Your home becomes a mess of dirty laundry, empty takeout containers, and unpaid bills. Showering, brushing your teeth, and doing your hair feel like a chore that you cannot bother with any longer.

What depression feels like at its most extreme is an utter lack of energy and motivation to do anything besides the absolute basics of bodily functions. If you have reached this stage, you need help.

A New Path Forward

Dealing with depression is not for the weak or fainthearted. It takes guts, determination, and a strong spirit. Regardless of what mistakes or bad choices you have made until this point, the fact that you are still here reading this shows what resilience you have. However, you don’t have to struggle alone. You are not the first person to battle depression, and you won’t be the last.

Start to develop good habits now by reaching out. Learn to identify your emotions and the patterns of your mental health to help you get ahead of your mood swings. Remember that every season becomes new. Even in the dead of winter, there is new life beneath the surface waiting for spring.

If you have never considered counseling before, now is the time to reach out. When you are ready, we hope that you will find a suitable counselor who can provide the encouragement and hope that is in Christ to live well as an image bearer of God. You can call to speak with our reception team, who will be delighted to help you find the help you need.

Photos:
“Sitting on the Field”, Courtesy of S W, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Standing in the Water”, Courtesy of Ben Iwara, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post What Depression Feels Like and How It Affects Your Life appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Your Anger
item.description:
Anger is a powerful emotion that can derail your life if you allow it. Not only can unbridled anger cloud your judgment, but it can also rob you of your sense of peace while damaging relationships, sometimes irreparably. As troublesome as it is, we should remember that anger isn’t necessarily sinful or against God’s will for our lives. Scripture reminds us, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” (Ephesians 4:26, ESV)

While anger isn’t necessarily sinful, the challenge that we all face is that anger can be difficult to manage. It’s way too easy for justifiable or righteous anger to quickly morph into the sort of anger that dishonors the Lord and others. What starts well and good can become damaging to your relational, emotional, and mental well-being. Having good anger management strategies can help you maintain a healthy balance.

Unpacking the Impact of Anger

When you feel anger rising inside of you, usually it’s because it’s been triggered by something. You may have been snubbed at work by a colleague, or your loved one left you feeling unheard. Perhaps someone took advantage of you, or you witnessed something manifestly unjust. Whatever it is, one of the emotional responses to such situations is anger, and that anger is often appropriate.

Anger can be overwhelming, and indulging it may seem so rewarding in the moment. Letting choice words fly at someone who cut you off in traffic can give you a sense of accomplishment or victory. I sure told them, we might say to ourselves. It is way too easy to go over the line and say too much, say something you regret, or act recklessly without regard to how those words or actions feel to other people.

It may be helpful to picture anger like a wild bronco that may have placid moments, but that can change in an instant. It’s not wise to turn your back or let your guard down around them. Uncontrolled anger can wreak havoc in your life by stirring up conflict, leading you to utter hurtful words you otherwise wouldn’t, or taking you down the path to actions you later regret.

There is a Proverb that says, “An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins.” (Proverbs 29:22, NIV) If anger begins controlling you, it becomes a chronic problem. Such anger has spiritual consequences, such as derailing your walk with the Lord (James 1:19-22). Chronic anger can also increase your stress levels and negatively impact your physical health by increasing your blood pressure and the risk of heart disease.

Besides these effects of uncontrolled anger, there can be a relational cost to anger, too. Anger can create deep wounds between loved ones, and those wounds can be slow to heal. Anger can also build walls between people, especially when that anger makes them feel unsafe around you. Anger, then, can be quite devastating.

The Blessings of Better Anger Management

The above probably gives anger a bad rap by pointing out all of the negative impacts of anger. Remember, anger isn’t sinful in itself. There is something to be said for dealing with anger in a healthy and constructive way. Anger can be a tool used for growth and renewal, and it’s not just destructive.

An example of this is when you feel unheard by a loved one. The feelings of anger can be handled well or poorly. The unhealthy route would include giving them the silent treatment in response or shouting at them to make yourself heard. The healthy option would include listening to that anger and discerning what lies at the root of it, and then pursuing dialogue with your loved one.

It is possible to express anger in healthy ways that build stronger relationships. Anger can function like a check engine light to let you know what’s happening inside you. Responding appropriately to those cues helps you communicate your needs effectively with others. This can mean fostering deeper trust and intimacy when you give gentle responses to tense situations.

Being in control of your anger and managing it well can also mean better health as you lower your stress levels, open yourself up more to the Lord’s peace, and yield more and more to the Spirit’s guidance. You’re better able to live well with yourself and with others when you can manage your emotions effectively.

Why Some Anger Management Strategies Fail

There are many benefits to managing your anger well. However, there are pitfalls along that path, and being aware of them can help you to be fruitful as you try to keep your anger in check.

Anger management strategies can fail or fall short when they are only skin deep. There is a strategy where you count slowly down from ten, and it’s a way to help you slow down before you respond rashly. This strategy does work in the moment, but it’s important to address the underlying heart issues. Anger can resurface and become harder to control.

Sticking with anger management strategies can also be difficult if you’re relying solely on willpower. For sustained and lasting change, we need the Lord’s help as well as accountability from others. The encouragement and support we get from other people can help us stay on the path, and the work of the Spirit in us can bring about true transformation in our hearts.

In other circumstances, anger management strategies don’t stick because we ignore the root causes of anger. Anger may be a momentary response, but many other things, such as learned patterns of behavior, often inform it. Other underlying causes of anger could be stress, unforgiveness, or unresolved trauma, which can fuel your anger and unhealthy responses to situations.

Awareness of these potential pitfalls can help you make good use of anger management strategies that help you keep anger in check. At the same time, you can address the deeper issues that could be informing your anger.

Effective Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Anger

There are many strategies that you can use to help you manage your anger. It’s important to remember that anger management isn’t about suppressing your anger or pretending it doesn’t exist. Those are different ways of handling anger poorly. Rather, the goal is to develop a healthy relationship with your anger, to be able to understand your own anger, and channel it constructively instead of letting it take the reins.

Some effective anger management strategies include the following:

Pause, and pray: Allow yourself to count down from ten, or to leave the room briefly when you can, to allow yourself space to calm down. Stepping out of the situation can make a difference. When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

Photos:
“Eruption”, Courtesy of Jonatan Pie, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Protesters”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; “Praying”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; 

The post Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Your Anger appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

There are many strategies that you can use to help you manage your anger. It’s important to remember that anger management isn’t about suppressing your anger or pretending it doesn’t exist. Those are different ways of handling anger poorly. Rather, the goal is to develop a healthy relationship with your anger, to be able to understand your own anger, and channel it constructively instead of letting it take the reins.

Some effective anger management strategies include the following:

Pause, and pray: Allow yourself to count down from ten, or to leave the room briefly when you can, to allow yourself space to calm down. Stepping out of the situation can make a difference. When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

item.description:

Not only can unbridled anger cloud your judgment, but it can also rob you of your sense of peace while damaging relationships, sometimes irreparably. As troublesome as it is, we should remember that anger isn’t necessarily sinful or against God’s will for our lives. Scripture reminds us, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” (Ephesians 4:26, ESV)

While anger isn’t necessarily sinful, the challenge that we all face is that anger can be difficult to manage. It’s way too easy for justifiable or righteous anger to quickly morph into the sort of anger that dishonors the Lord and others. What starts well and good can become damaging to your relational, emotional, and mental well-being. Having good anger management strategies can help you maintain a healthy balance.

Unpacking the Impact of Anger

When you feel anger rising inside of you, usually it’s because it’s been triggered by something. You may have been snubbed at work by a colleague, or your loved one left you feeling unheard. Perhaps someone took advantage of you, or you witnessed something manifestly unjust. Whatever it is, one of the emotional responses to such situations is anger, and that anger is often appropriate.

Anger can be overwhelming, and indulging it may seem so rewarding in the moment. Letting choice words fly at someone who cut you off in traffic can give you a sense of accomplishment or victory. I sure told them, we might say to ourselves. It is way too easy to go over the line and say too much, say something you regret, or act recklessly without regard to how those words or actions feel to other people.

It may be helpful to picture anger like a wild bronco that may have placid moments, but that can change in an instant. It’s not wise to turn your back or let your guard down around them. Uncontrolled anger can wreak havoc in your life by stirring up conflict, leading you to utter hurtful words you otherwise wouldn’t, or taking you down the path to actions you later regret.

There is a Proverb that says, “An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins.” (Proverbs 29:22, NIV) If anger begins controlling you, it becomes a chronic problem. Such anger has spiritual consequences, such as derailing your walk with the Lord (James 1:19-22). Chronic anger can also increase your stress levels and negatively impact your physical health by increasing your blood pressure and the risk of heart disease.

Besides these effects of uncontrolled anger, there can be a relational cost to anger, too. Anger can create deep wounds between loved ones, and those wounds can be slow to heal. Anger can also build walls between people, especially when that anger makes them feel unsafe around you. Anger, then, can be quite devastating.

The Blessings of Better Anger Management

The above probably gives anger a bad rap by pointing out all of the negative impacts of anger. Remember, anger isn’t sinful in itself. There is something to be said for dealing with anger in a healthy and constructive way. Anger can be a tool used for growth and renewal, and it’s not just destructive.

An example of this is when you feel unheard by a loved one. The feelings of anger can be handled well or poorly. The unhealthy route would include giving them the silent treatment in response or shouting at them to make yourself heard. The healthy option would include listening to that anger and discerning what lies at the root of it, and then pursuing dialogue with your loved one.

It is possible to express anger in healthy ways that build stronger relationships. Anger can function like a check engine light to let you know what’s happening inside you. Responding appropriately to those cues helps you communicate your needs effectively with others. This can mean fostering deeper trust and intimacy when you give gentle responses to tense situations.

Being in control of your anger and managing it well can also mean better health as you lower your stress levels, open yourself up more to the Lord’s peace, and yield more and more to the Spirit’s guidance. You’re better able to live well with yourself and with others when you can manage your emotions effectively.

Why Some Anger Management Strategies Fail

There are many benefits to managing your anger well. However, there are pitfalls along that path, and being aware of them can help you to be fruitful as you try to keep your anger in check.

Anger management strategies can fail or fall short when they are only skin deep. There is a strategy where you count slowly down from ten, and it’s a way to help you slow down before you respond rashly. This strategy does work in the moment, but it’s important to address the underlying heart issues. Anger can resurface and become harder to control.

Sticking with anger management strategies can also be difficult if you’re relying solely on willpower. For sustained and lasting change, we need the Lord’s help as well as accountability from others. The encouragement and support we get from other people can help us stay on the path, and the work of the Spirit in us can bring about true transformation in our hearts.

In other circumstances, anger management strategies don’t stick because we ignore the root causes of anger. Anger may be a momentary response, but many other things, such as learned patterns of behavior, often inform it. Other underlying causes of anger could be stress, unforgiveness, or unresolved trauma, which can fuel your anger and unhealthy responses to situations.

Awareness of these potential pitfalls can help you make good use of anger management strategies that help you keep anger in check. At the same time, you can address the deeper issues that could be informing your anger.

Effective Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Anger

When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

item.title: The Purpose of Mindfulness in Counseling
item.description:
In the world of counseling psychology and therapy, the concept of mindfulness has been growing in both popularity and interest over the last several decades. As this trend has grown, researchers have brought additional evidence to support the use of mindfulness practices in counseling and therapy sessions.

In this article, I’d like to bring attention to the effectiveness of mindfulness, some of the clinical evidence that supports its use, as well as some practical techniques, trauma-informed applications, and how we can integrate mindfulness practices into our Christian spiritual formation.

Before we dive into some of the particularities of mindfulness, let’s first answer the question, “What is mindfulness?”

Mindfulness is a practice that asks the participant to deliberately and intentionally focus his/her attention on their present experience in a nonjudgmental way. Furthermore, mindfulness is a state that helps individuals become more aware of physical, mental, and emotional conditions without judgment. In other words, it can be described as a state of focused attention, paying particular attention to the moment, in a nonjudgmental way.

Clinical Evidence for the Use of Mindfulness Techniques

Research done through the American Counseling Association found that mindfulness is used in the treatment of a variety of mental-health concerns such as intellectual disorders, autism spectrum, trauma, eating disorders, anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, and sexual dysfunction disorders. Additionally, mindfulness techniques can be paired with different therapeutic modalities to enhance the healing process and spur on deeper transformation.

An article published by Positive Psychology states that mindfulness (through mindfulness-based interventions) changes neural pathways in the brain related to rumination, worry, self-regulation, compassion, attention, emotional reactivity, and affect.

Put more simply, clinical evidence shows that the practice of mindfulness helps change your brain’s thinking patterns. Furthermore, it changes the structure of your brain’s neural pathways, which ultimately allows you to change what you think about and how you think.

In my own work with clients, mindfulness practices have started to become a regular part of my practice. By facilitating a moment to pause and bring attention to the moment by noticing breathing patterns, what sensations are occurring in the body, and what emotions are present, clients commonly express experiencing a greater depth of calm.

This is because mindfulness techniques and practices not only impact the brain, but also the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the nervous system. These intricate internal systems are also responsible for connecting to deeper sensations of relaxation and stress relief.

Practical Ways That Mindfulness Can Be Used

Some of the most common mindfulness practices and techniques involve your attention and your breath. Since we live in such a fast-paced world, it can be easy to lose sight of the moment. Our minds are constantly thinking about “the next thing.” Or we’re scrolling on our phones, responding to texts, emails, or social media posts. With our attention consistently being drawn elsewhere, mindfulness seeks to slow us down (in a positive way).

Our breath is an easy access point or signal to our internal states, or what’s happening inside of us. Our breath is also always with us (thank God) and isn’t something we have to dig for. By beginning to focus attention on the breath, the mind can begin to settle, not rushing from one thing to another. Your breath is present with you. Your body is present with you. God is present with you.

As mentioned earlier, focused and nonjudgmental attention are two major tenets in mindfulness practices. We are often our harshest critics. When the inner critic becomes too loud, mindfulness can help you reset your thoughts and feelings to help you not get stuck in your head. Here is a basic outline you can use:

Breath Take one minute and focus on your breathing pattern. What characteristics do you notice? Is your breathing shallow or is it deep? Don’t try to change your breathing; just notice it.

Action Ask yourself the question, “Is there a particular action that my body is wanting to do right now?” As you sit with your breath and this question, notice what comes to mind.

Sensation Continuing to breathe, ask yourself, “What sensations am I experiencing in my body right now?” Take a minute to notice these sensations and where you feel them.

Emotion Continuing to breathe, take one more minute to notice what emotions you’re feeling on the inside. Joy? Frustration? Sadness? Again, you shouldn’t be judging what you’re feeling, simply noticing.

An exercise like this can be done in about 4-5 minutes, get you in touch with your body and your nervous system, and promote a deeper sense of regulation.

Trauma-Informed Applications of Mindfulness Practices

For someone who has experienced trauma, one of the most important things in recovery is helping the person to be grounded in the moment. Traumatic events commonly cause someone to flee from the moment.

This is because their body (aka their nervous system) had a sense that being present in the specific trauma would have been too painful for them to bear. However, when the person is no longer in that specific traumatic moment, their nervous system may still be holding onto the belief that anywhere is safer than the moment.

This is why mindfulness practices can be so incredibly effective and helpful in trauma recovery. By practicing mindfulness – a state of focused attention, paying particular attention to the moment, in a nonjudgmental way – the person is essentially retraining their own nervous system to trust that the moment is safe.

The purpose of helping those who have experienced trauma be grounded in the moment is to anchor them back into reality. When a person is legitimately triggered, their brain and nervous system cannot tell the difference between the present and the past.

Often the person begins to act, feel, and think as if they’re actually back in the traumatic situation. As they become flooded with distress, their nervous system begins to kick into overdrive, propelling them to try anything and everything to get back to a place of safety both emotionally and physically.

Using mindfulness practices in this instance helps the person orient themselves to the reality they’re actually in. Some of these include the 5-4-3-2-1 Method, which invites the person to look around them and name five things they can see, four they can touch, etc. Another includes a breathing method like the 4-7-8 technique. Each exercise is designed to ground the person in the present and reduce distress in the nervous system.

How does mindfulness integrate with faith in God?

There are many contemplative Christian spiritual practices that can be intertwined with using mindfulness in counseling and throughout the day. The majority of these practices revolve around prayer. Two examples of this are what is known as Listening Prayer and Meditative Prayer (Christian Meditation).

It is important to note here that secular mindfulness practice often focuses on emptying the mind in order to find or attain peace. Christian meditative practices, however, focus on stilling oneself in the presence of God to be filled with His presence and listen for His voice. The goal of each is the same: hear God’s voice and be filled by Him.

Listening Prayer is exactly what it sounds like: a posture of prayer where someone is listening for God’s voice. Jamie and Donna Winship are an excellent resource if you’re interested in learning more about this practice. Here is a simple four-step model you can use to start out or grow in this practice:

Be still Quiet yourself in the presence of God.

Be looking Look for a vision or pictures in your mind as you pray and seek God.

Be listening God’s voice often comes as the free flow of thoughts that light upon your mind as you’re focusing your attention on Jesus.

Be writing Write out the free flow of thoughts, pictures, images that come as you’re focusing on Jesus.

Again, the emphasis here is that attention is being focused on Jesus. This is not an exercise to empty the mind, but rather to shift focused attention and train our hearts and minds to seek Jesus.

Christian Meditation is another prayer model used with the goal of quieting ourselves in God’s presence to hear from Him and be filled by Him. This is ultimately to grow closer to God. Hallow is an app that helps people walk through the practice of Christian Meditation. Here are some of the steps they have outlined:

Find a comfortable place to pray God meets us where we are – it doesn’t have to be perfect. Just make sure you feel like you can be yourself with God in this place, whether you’re alone or in public.

Prepare your heart and mind for prayer Think about your prayer before starting to pray. Is there anything on my mind that I want to offer to God in prayer? Are there things preventing me from resting with God?

Select a prayer, verse, or word to meditate on In Christian meditation, we always meditate on something holy that will fill our hearts and bring us closer to God.

Let God fill your heart Remember: it’s not as much about what we say in prayer but how well we prepare ourselves to listen to God’s voice in the silence.

End with thanksgiving and gratitude Conclude your time in prayer by thanking God for this time with you.

As we come to the end, I hope that you’re leaving with a better understanding of the usefulness of practicing mindfulness and how it can be applied in various aspects of your life. As a counselor, these are tools I enjoy integrating into my work with clients.

If reading this article sparked your interest or curiosity, I would love to hear from you! I am currently taking on new clients in both Green Lake and Bothell locations, as well as online throughout Washington State.

item.title: What Are the Different Attachment Types and Why Do They Matter?
item.description:
Attachment Theory

In this modern age of pop psychology, many people are starting to hear about attachment theory. Some may even be able to tell you their exact attachment style. If you’re new to the idea of attachment theory, you may be curious about exactly what it is and what purpose it serves.

John Bowlby, a psychologist from the mid-twentieth century, founded the idea of Attachment Theory. In the 1950s, he described attachment behavior as behavior whereby an individual attains or maintains a connection to another clearly identified individual seen as better able to cope with the world (Bowlby, 1982).

Another psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, later tested his theory of connection with infants ranging from 9-30 months in age to see how they would react to short periods of separation from their caregivers (Ainsworth, 1978). Her findings, and the findings of later studies, informed the types of attachment styles and how these styles impact both children and adults.

Types of Attachment Style

“Attachment styles comprise cognitions relating to both the self (‘Am I worthy of love’) and others (‘Can I depend on others during times of stress’)” (Huang, 2026). Attachments begin in infancy. God designed us this way.

Consider the beginning of Scripture where God says, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.” (Gen. 2:18, ESV BibleGateway.com). God’s original plan was to have a right relationship with Him and with others, just as He is in relationship with Himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Unfortunately, due to sin entering the world, our relationships with others are not perfect. Because of this, while secure attachments do exist, there are three types of attachment styles that are insecure: anxious-preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, and disorganized, otherwise known as fearful-avoidant. The following excerpt from Simply Psychology has a breakdown of each:

Secure Attachment: Securely attached individuals are comfortable with intimacy and can balance dependence and independence in relationships.

Preoccupied Attachment (Anxious in Children): Individuals with this attachment style crave intimacy and can be overly dependent and demanding in relationships.

Dismissive Attachment (Avoidant in Children): This style is characterized by a strong sense of self-sufficiency, often to the point of appearing detached. Individuals with dismissive attachment value their independence highly and may seem uninterested in close relationships.

Fearful Attachment (Disorganized in Children): Individuals with a fearful attachment style desire close relationships and fear vulnerability. They may behave unpredictably in relationships due to their internal conflict between a desire for intimacy and fear of it (Huang, 2026).

A further breakdown of the behaviors that help identify each attachment style is as follows:

Secure

  • Healthy communication and management of conflict
  • Healthy view of self, others, and God
  • Regulated emotions
  • Ability to trust and connect with self, others, and God
  • Feeling comfortable alone
  • Being emotionally available for others

Anxious-Preoccupied

  • Feeling unworthy of connection
  • Highly sensitive to criticism
  • Uncomfortable with being alone
  • Low self-esteem
  • Difficulty with trusting self, others, or God
  • Feelings of jealousy
  • Fearing rejection or abandonment

Dismissive-Avoidant

  • Strong sense of independence
  • Easily dismiss others
  • Difficulty with trusting others or God
  • Avoiding emotional or physical intimacy
  • Having issues with commitment

Fearful-Avoidant

  • Having difficulty trusting self, others, and God
  • Struggling to regulate emotions
  • Showing signs of both anxious and avoidant attachment styles
  • Fearing rejection
  • Showing signs of confusing and contradictory behaviors (Cleveland Clinic, 2026).

Examples of Each Attachment in the Bible

Forming attachments is an unavoidable part of the human experience. Whether we have a secure or insecure attachment, the type we possess has wide-ranging consequences for how we view ourselves, others, and even how we view God. The following biblical figures map these styles with startling accuracy:

Secure

Ruth, who followed Naomi after the death of her husband and entrusted herself to Naomi and to God.

“Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” – Ruth 1:16, ESV

John, the beloved disciple of Jesus, to whom Jesus entrusted his mother.

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold your son!’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold your mother!’ And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. – John 19:26-27, ESV

Anxious-Preoccupied

King David, who openly expresses throughout the Psalms his fear and anxiety of being abandoned by God.

“O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me…O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes – it also has gone from me…Do not forsake me, O Lord! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!” – Psalm 38:1-2, 9-10, 21-22, ESV

Dismissive-Avoidant

Jonah, who, at God’s call to witness to the Ninevites, fled the complete opposite direction.

Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.’ But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord. – Jonah 1:1-3, ESV

Fearful-Avoidant

The nation of Israel after God saved them from the Egyptians, led them with pillars of cloud and fire, gave them water in the desert, and fed them manna from heaven.

Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, ‘You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die.’ – Exodus 20:18-19, ESV

While these are exemplary models of specific attachments, I do not mean to suggest that these people can be universally typed according to Attachment Theory. Rather, these examples model known attachment behaviors and are thus useful for informing this article.

What is Earned Secure Attachment?

If you have read through and identified with any of the insecure attachment behaviors, the good news is that your attachment is not set in stone. Whether you had a difficult childhood that has led to trust issues, fear, and anxiety, or whether adult relationships have damaged your sense of self and trust in God and others, healing is possible.

Through therapy, forming healthy relationships, prayer, and practicing gentle self-reflection, you can build an earned secure attachment style.

But what exactly does “earned secure” mean, and what does it look like? A person with an earned secure attachment has “achieved a secure relationship with their own story. They can discuss their past clearly, acknowledge its impact on them, and hold their early caregivers with a mixture of realism and compassion – without being overwhelmed by grief, dismissive of the experience, or incoherent when describing it. (Simply Psychology, 2026).

EMDR, Lifespan Integration, Internal Family Systems (IFS), or other attachment-based therapies have proven effective in healing attachment wounds and moving clients toward forming stronger, healthier relationships with self, God, and others.

If you’ve found this article helpful in identifying an insecure attachment in yourself, it is never too late to take the first steps toward transforming how you view yourself, others, and even how you view God. God wants you to live life to the full. Therapy can help you get started.

References:
Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of attachment: A psychological study of the strange situation. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.
Bowlby, J. (1982). Attachment and loss: Retrospect and prospect. American Journal of Orthopsychiatry, 52(4), 664–678. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-0025.1982.tb01456.x
Huang, S. (2026, April 20). Attachment styles in relationships. Simply Psychology. https://www.simplypsychology.org/attachment-styles.html
Professional, C. C. M. (2026, February 13). Attachment styles. Cleveland Clinic. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/25170-attachment-styles
Simply Psychology. (2026, May 15). Earned Secure attachment: How adults can develop a secure attachment style. https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/earned-secure- attachment
